"It was June 1984," he writes, "and I had just been forced to file for bankruptcy. The newspapers were saying that I had lost eight million dollars and that much of it had gone up my nose. . . . My band, Fleetwood Mac, once one of the biggest groups in the world, hadn't played together in two years." In "Fleetwood," a blithe, slapdash memoir written with Stephen Davis, the author of "Hammer of the Gods," Mr. Fleetwood makes the rock musician's life seem cliched and ho-hum: he needed to play music, he made too much money, he took too many drugs. Fleetwood Mac, begun in England in the summer of 1967, has undergone several incarnations over the last two decades in both its music and its personnel. However, the most significant change came in 1975, when Mr. Fleetwood hired the singer-songwriters Stevie Nicks and Lindsey Buckingham. This edition of the band -- "more powerful than ever," Mr. Fleetwood writes -- would produce a string of best-selling albums. The downside was that the band began to abuse cocaine. "Until then, Fleetwood Mac hadn't had much experience with this Andean rocket fuel," he writes. "Now we discovered that a toot now and then relieved the boredom of long hours in the studio with little nourishment." Mr. Fleetwood, the band's manager as well as its drummer, says he felt compelled to get the other members to carry on with their work. After he recouped his financial losses in 1985, Mr. Fleetwood and the band gave it one more go, and in 1987 they released one last hit album before Mr. Buckingham left. Mr. Fleetwood has since recast the band yet again and looks forward to more life on the road. "I'll keep playing forever," he writes. "I'm going to be an eighty-year-old rocker, and they'll have to take me out and shoot me to get me to stop."

title: Lovingly, Georgia
author: Anita Pollitzer
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: LOVINGLY, GEORGIA: The Complete Correspondence of Georgia O'Keeffe & Anita Pollitzer.  Edited by Clive Giboire. (Touchstone, Cloth, $24.95; Paper, $14.95.) "Lovingly Georgia" is more than the complete correspondence between Georgia O'Keeffe and Anita Pollitzer, a friend and fellow artist with whom O'Keeffe exchanged letters for 53 years. It is also the story of a friendship broken after years of affinity and trust. O'Keeffe and Pollitzer met at Columbia University in 1914. Over the next several years, as O'Keeffe took teaching jobs in Virginia, South Carolina and Texas, the two corresponded almost weekly. Lonely and at times depressed, O'Keeffe found in Pollitzer's exuberant letters a link to the world she had left behind. Pollitzer sent books, photographs, art supplies and the latest avant-garde magazines, shared her thoughts on writers and critics, and described plays, art exhibits and lectures she had seen. O'Keeffe was equally expressive, though her letters spoke not of social events or of art ideas but of the huge Texas sky or a lightning storm at night on the prairie. She wrote of her daily schedule, of being lost in her work, unsure of her sanity. In Pollitzer she found not only a sympathetic ear but also an ardent supporter, critic and agent. O'Keeffe periodically sent Pollitzer rolls of drawings, to which she responded with unabashed enthusiasm. "It screams like a maniac & runs around like a dog chasing his tail," she exclaimed of one picture. "They've gotten past the personal stage into the big sort of emotions that are common to big people," she wrote of other works. Both women thought that the most important place to show art was at Alfred Stieglitz' gallery. Without telling her friend, Pollitzer took O'Keeffe's drawings to Stieglitz, whose now legendary response, "Finally a woman on paper," would change O'Keeffe's life. Stieglitz showed O'Keeffe's work and later married her. In 1950, with O'Keeffe's approval, Pollitzer began work on a biography. As the last of the letters in "Lovingly, Georgia" shows, the project came to a bad end after 18 years. (The book, edited by Clive Giboire -- who is also the editor of this volume -- was posthumously published in 1988 as "A Woman on Paper: Georgia O'Keeffe.") "I cannot approve it . . . in any way," wrote O'Keeffe. "It is a very sentimental way you like to imagine me," she observed. "It reads as if we . . . didn't understand one another at all." Yet to judge from the depth and candor of these fascinating letters, O'Keeffe's disavowal seems not only cruel but a denial of the rapport these two women so obviously shared.
headline: Georgia on Her Mind

title: The Plains Of Passage
author: Jean M Auel
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE PLAINS OF PASSAGE.  By Jean M. Auel (Crown, $24.95.) Prehistory buffs may be the only readers who'll have fun with Jean M. Auel's latest epic, "The Plains of Passage." In this fourth installment of the Earth's Children series, the adventure begun in "The Clan of the Cave Bear" continues, with Ayla of the Mamutoi and Jondalar of the Zelandonii undertaking a long and tortuous journey on horseback across the wind-swept grasslands of Ice Age Europe in search of Jondalar's kin. Will the two travelers ever reach the camp of the Zelandonii and, if they do, will Jondalar's fellow clansmen recognize him after so long an absence? These questions haunt Jondalar and Ayla throughout the novel, but a more pressing challenge is posed by the natural world that surrounds them, which sets a host of dangers in their path. Although Ms. Auel's descriptions of this world are fairly uninspired, the steamy love scenes between Ayla and Jondalar afford some compensation. Yet these interludes are few and far between, and it's unlikely that all but the most devoted readers will follow them to the book's end. Prehistory buffs with any savvy will also find Ms. Auel's feminist portrayal of the blond, blue-eyed Ayla somewhat hard to swallow. Here is a multilingual woman who, among other talents, is clever enough to invent a contraceptive, in an era when human reproductive capabilities were apparently still a mystery to mankind. Such skills may enhance Ayla's status in the novel -- but among readers they're apt to raise a few eyebrows.

author: Harold Pinter
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE DWARFS.  By Harold Pinter. (Grove Weidenfeld, $17.95.) It comes as little surprise to discover that Harold Pinter's only novel is composed almost entirely of dialogue. "The Dwarfs" was completed in the early 1950's, before Mr. Pinter wrote any of his plays, before he established himself as one of the most influential voices of his generation. The delayed appearance of "The Dwarfs" is certainly a literary event. Nevertheless, it's easy to see why the novel has taken over 30 years to arrive, and why Mr. Pinter himself told The Paris Review in 1967 that it was "not good enough to be published, really." While some of the original material has evidently been cut and rearranged, what remains can be ferociously vague at times and woefully sophomoric at others. To be sure, a calculated ambiguity combined with a wealth of non sequiturs and a dearth of action emerge as powerful aspects of Mr. Pinter's theater of menace, and scholars will enjoy finding signs of his later work in this preliminary exercise. But such techniques do not make for a compelling novel. (Nor did they succeed, as Mr. Pinter also once acknowledged, when he based a play on "The Dwarfs" in 1960.) The story, if it can be called that, hovers around four characters. Pete, the catalyst, is a reluctant moralist given to internal musings a la Joyce and Beckett. He apparently works in some kind of an office, perhaps involved with "literary research." Though we learn that Virginia is a teacher, that Mark is an actor and a Lothario, and that Len works in an industrial setting, such information is outside Mr. Pinter's existential concerns. In its relentlessly dialectical unfolding, "The Dwarfs" aims to capture nothing less than "this whole bloody racket" called life. As the novel progresses, Mr. Pinter's characters might be accused of simply evaporating -- if they'd ever come into focus in the first place. Throughout, they remain blurry figures, four characters in search of the playwright Mr. Pinter would become, and in need of actors to embody the inflated ideas they represent.

title: Real Life Drama
author: Wendy Smith
outlet: The New York Times
pull_quote: Real Life Drama The Group Theater and America, 1931-1940 By Wendy Smith Illustrated. 482 pages. Alfred A. Knopf. $24.95.   Many memoirs have been written about the theatrical company that in the 1930's tried to revolutionize American culture. The best known of them are probably "The Fervent Years: The Story of the Group Theater and the 30's" (Harcourt Brace Jovanovich), by Harold Clurman, one of the company's three founding directors, and "Elia Kazan: A Life" (Knopf), by the Group's most famously successful graduate.   But never before has the whole story been told as meticulously and objectively as Wendy Smith has done in her exhaustive "Real Life Drama: The Group Theater and America, 1931-1940." Recognizing in the Group's passionate intensity the sense of political commitment she herself felt in the turbulent 1960's, Ms. Smith has immersed herself in her subject's yearnings and traced its chronicle from start to finish. Unfortunately, her zeal outpaces her ability to breathe life into her story.      The Group Theater's history comprised some two dozen Broadway productions of wildly varying success, annual summer retreats to the country during which the Group members worked at their stage techniques, and endless tergiversation.  Luckily for the content of "Real Life Drama," two of the Group's founders, Harold Clurman and Lee Strasberg, stood for important dramaturgical ideals that tended toward opposing poles. (This is in no way meant to slight the third founder, Cheryl Crawford, who somewhat too selflessly took on most of the practical details of sustaining the Group's existence.)   As Ms. Smith summarizes one of Harold Clurman's early "rambling, impassioned lectures": "From his statement of principles, Clurman drew two main conclusions. They had to do with the twin imperatives of art -- form and content -- and it was typical of the sharply contrasting personalities of the two men who pulled their group in often uneasy tandem for seven years that form was Strasberg's bailiwick and content was Clurman's."   Form was essentially acting style, which Strasberg permanently changed in America. Drawing on the techniques developed by Konstantin Stanislavsky in his Moscow Art Theater, Strasberg taught the Group's actors how to build a stage character from their psychic interiors rather than depend on the illusion of physical gesture. Fittingly enough, as Ms. Smith observes, Strasberg's acting revolution came to fruition with the Method style of the self-absorbed 1950's, long after the socially committed 30's. It is a style from which audiences continue to benefit in the best of contemporary cinematic acting.     Content, on the other hand, had to do with the material that the actors performed. Clurman dreamed of turning the Group into a school for content, an institution that would not only embody the political and cultural issues of the day but also develop playwrights to dramatize those issues. Alas for American theater history, all he got for his trouble was Clifford Odets.   True, the passages describing Odets's work with the Group provide the few exciting moments of "Real Life Drama." On the night in January 1935 when his famous taxi-strike play, "Waiting for Lefty," opened, the playwright, the actors and the audience achieved the "near-religious communion" of which Clurman dreamed. And subsequent productions of Odets's "Awake and Sing!" and "Paradise Lost" must have come as close as anything the Group experienced to what the Moscow Art Theater achieved in its productions of the plays of Chekhov.   But the fact of the matter is that the best of Odets falls far short of Chekhov. Had the Group come up with even a Eugene O'Neill, its history might have been different. Perhaps to have produced a great playwright was impossible, given the stridently political issues of the times.  Whether to go on strike is hardly material for important drama. But in any case the Group didn't, and without a major artist to lead it, it was bound to falter.     Ms. Smith admits "that many of the Group's most famous efforts haven't aged well." She adds: "It's possible to read 'Lefty' and still be moved by its passion, but it's doubtful that it could be performed today with any credibility. The other Odets plays    can    be done, . . . but too often they're turgid and stagy, with the actors and directors unable to find any living significance in scripts written 50 years ago."   But she neglects to imagine what the nurturing of a great playwright might have meant to the Group, how the birth of a native Sophocles, Shakespeare, Moliere, Ibsen or Brecht might have lifted the company with an innovative, visionary body of drama. Instead she blames the fragility of human relations, and documents their failure endlessly in earnest but drab prose.   Was the Group's work worth all the trouble? On balance, it seems to have been. As Ms. Smith sums up: "A distinguished list of productions offered over 10 years; an acting technique that remains enormously influential; a new emphasis on ordinary experience -- these were the Group's specific contributions to the American theater, and they weren't trivial ones."     And as Eunice Stoddard, an original member of the Group, eloquently testifies: "Everybody had their frustrations. I stayed because it was more interesting theater than anywhere else. Rehearsals were always so exciting: the whole analysis of the play, of the parts, of what the play was saying in terms of our era, was just so much more stimulating than anything you'd ever get on Broadway. You didn't want to leave that for what you knew you'd be getting outside, which might satisfy your ego as an actress but not necessarily create very interesting theater. It was a very difficult choice."   But "Real Life Drama" doesn't live up to its author's passion for her subject. Her zealous devotion comes through, but it remains by and large uninspired and uninspiring.

title: Pheasants Of The Mind
author: Datus C Proper
outlet: The New York Times
pull_quote: Pheasants of the Mind  By Datus C. Proper  Illustrated. 154 pages. Prentice Hall Press. $18.95.     The subject is birds, seasonably enough, though it is pheasants not turkeys that Datus C. Proper would kill and dress and cook for his Thanksgiving table. Or his Christmas table. Or his table in any season of the year, as he testifies eloquently in "Pheasants of the Mind: A Hunter's Search for a Mythic Bird."   A retired Foreign Service officer who now lives in Bozeman, Mont., Mr. Proper (rhymes with roper) is a writer who hunts, not the other way around. On a typical day described in "Pheasants," he will be typing away when Huckleberry, his "domesticated wolf" will wriggle his muzzle under his elbow and let him know that "an ear-rub would be welcome." The ear-rub soon leads to a fetched boot and a dance "on crooked hind legs, like the god Pan."   "Huckleberry wants to go hunting," Mr. Proper writes. "He wants it because it is in his genes. I want it because it is in my genes. The hunting game makes no sense, these days, but it still feels as if it ought to." Pheasants are the author's game because they are to birds what the brown trout is to fish, which is important, as readers of the author's earlier book, "What the Trout Said" (Alfred A. Knopf), will understand.     As Mr. Proper explains in his new book: both pheasants and brown trout "had been learning about civilization for centuries before arriving in this country.   "Both species flaunted their knowledge. The old-world trout would sip real insects while refusing the angler's flies. The old-world bird would stand in a field looking heroic, then disappear when the hunter got out of his car."    But you can catch a fish and put it back. A shotgunned pheasant doesn't live to flush another day. As Alexander Pope wrote in "Windsor Forest":     See! from the brake the whirring pheasant springs,   And mounts exulting on triumphant wings:   Short is his joy; he feels the fiery wound,   Flutters in blood, and panting beats the ground.      What would make a writer and fisherman want to kill a bird?   Mr. Proper replies: "I want to give the cock a better death than he might get from other predators. Call it a deal: I deprive him of time, spare him from being eaten alive. He would not take the deal if he had a choice, but it's the best I can offer."     Some deal. But the author goes to lengths to make one understand. The pheasant is charming to his eye: "The cock's coat of many colors is also a nature jacket. His habitat is bronze grass, green leaves, bright shafts of light, and deep shadows. His colors are an elegant solution.   "Looking at all of the American upland birds without sentiment (a kind of apostasy), I reckon now that the cock pheasant is the most beautiful. He is a trompe-l'oeil masterpiece of a kind that even nature does not often produce."    So pheasants haunt his mind. His mind works something like this, if one may elide a subtle argument. Hunting is walking; walking is thinking; thinking is language; language is a beat. "By the time you hear the beat," Mr. Proper writes, "the thing that caused it has become important.  It    must    be important to have done this to you. Therefore you try very hard to shoot the bird when your chance comes. You try even if you were not eager when you started walking. If you have not had the experience, you may find this baffling, but I imagine the long-distance hunters nodding yes, yes."     Even if this is baffling, Mr. Proper discourses upon the habitats in which pheasants should be hunted, the right dog to point them, the right weapon to carry, the right clothes to wear, the right way to cook the bird once you have brought him home.   For him pheasants are also dragons:    "When I slay the pheasant, I kill, first, the dragon in me, which is the ugly one appearing in most Western art. . . . I clutch this reality as an antidote to indifference. We think of hunting and fishing as escape, and they are. They are escape from a society of escapism: from pervasive complacency, from media pitched to the lowest common denominator, from trivialization of thought, from the politics of blandness, from gladiators, celebrities, entertainment, scandals, the life synthetic. A hunter chasing pheasants feels everything except anomie."   Well, this is putting quite a burden on what is basically a gaudy chicken.  But between his flights of prose Mr. Proper keeps coming back to genes:   " '. . . one kills in order to have hunted' (Ortega y Gasset)'   'One eats in order to have killed' (Proper)."     So perhaps "Pheasants of the Mind" is simply a necessary book, one that beautifully explains why people and game birds are the way they are. It certainly is attractively designed, and handsomely illustrated by Eldridge Hardie. And intriguing to read. Though on the whole I'd prefer the author stuck to the sport of fishing.

title: Nordi'S Gift
author: Clyde Rice
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: NORDI'S GIFT.  By Clyde Rice. (Breitenbush Books, $21.95.) Is man meant to spend life with only one mate? Can a literate person satisfy his intellect through the exhilaration of outdoor physical labor? Clyde Rice tussles with these questions throughout "Nordi's Gift," the sequel to his first volume of autobiography, "A Heaven in the Eye." In this volume, the author, now 87 years old, recounts his experiences from 1934 to 1955, and his vivacious writing conveys the passion and immediacy of his younger years. Mr. Rice revels in jobs that demand muscle -- he chopped and sold cordwood, repaired ships, built a boat and fished for tuna, opened a lumber mill. The book's most enthralling passages are devoted to the author's family. His strong voice and remarkable memory combine to produce finely wrought portraits of his wife, Nordi, and her niece, Virginia, with whom Mr. Rice fell in love. Readers may wonder about and even condemn some of the author's decisions. He divorced Nordi to marry Virginia; Nordi later lived with the new couple. (If that sounds strange, imagine working on and off, as Mr. Rice did, for a stepmother who despises you and a father easily swayed by his spouse.) As a social history of the American Northwest (Mr. Rice is a native of Oregon), "Nordi's Gift" makes for engrossing reading -- with one caveat. Adept with an ax, Mr. Rice cuts trees more easily than he cuts through prose. Too many technical descriptions of logging and shipbuilding impede his story. Yet Clyde Rice is good company and has written an inspiring book about a thoughtfully considered life.
headline: IN SHORT/SMALL PRESSES: NONFICTION

title: I Hear Voices
author: Paul Ableman
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: I HEAR VOICES.  By Paul Ableman. (McPherson, Cloth, $18; Paper, $10.) Paul Ableman, an esteemed British playwright and critic, originally published this arresting and brilliant travesty 30 years ago. His first novel (Mr. Ableman has published four more since), "I Hear Voices" originally appeared on the list of the Olympia Press, the Paris house that first brought out "Lolita" and "Naked Lunch." It may be read as one long wake-up call -- the protagonist never entirely makes it out of bed. The delivery of his breakfast egg is a recurrent set piece, and would be a symbol in a less explosive exercise. But Mr. Ableman must constantly break his eggs, fragment his abbreviated roundabout world. His unnamed narrator -- who, one quickly suspects, is a schizophrenic -- tumbles through a series of encounters that flare with offhand intensity, including a number of party scenes that seem startlingly canny about social give and take, despite their strangeness. Along the way, poetic tangents fly off in every direction: "There were far reports and others that leapt from brain to brain so that the sunset was pricked with doubt and signaled a spectrum of confused acknowledgement." Is this in fact the mind of a madman? There are scenes that suggest psychiatric counseling, but whatever grasp on reality they might offer is laughingly undone by the narrator's phantoms and leitmotifs. Mr. Ableman's best effect is a breathtaking precision about states of mind, played off against a hilarious vagueness about physical reality. His unchaptered slice of dream (occasionally reminiscent of Donald Barthelme) is another example of the wild freedoms embraced by European fiction since 1945, freedoms still only fitfully understood on this side of the Atlantic.
headline: The Breakfast Egg

title: The Woman Who Read Novels And Peacetime
author: Andy Brumer
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE WOMAN WHO READ NOVELS AND PEACETIME.  By Constance Urdang. (Coffee House Press, Paper, $9.95.) Constance Urdang, the author of five previous novellas as well as five books of verse, clearly displays a poet's sensitivity and depth of feeling in these two wonderfully crafted novellas. Leaning stylistically toward the experimental (though not tilting as far as the avant-garde), Ms. Urdang's crisp, angular prose explores the complexities of both loneliness and intimate relationships. "The Woman Who Read Novels," which is set in New York City, wanders between the past and present experiences of an elderly woman named Ruby, whose broken engagement to her cousin, Leo, has shadowed her life since she was barely past her teens. Alive with sadness, this novella depicts the chilling figure of a soul isolated and in despair. In contrast, the second novella -- titled, somewhat ironically, "Peacetime" -- presents the stories of several baby boomers who, while nostalgic for the 1960's and their idealized days as student activists, find their present-day marriages and close friendships enveloped in a fog of incompetence, violence and dread. Whereas "The Woman Who Read Novels" ends on a clearly pessimistic note, the very sense of failure felt by the characters in "Peacetime," their struggle to make satisfying contact with others, propel them forward in a heroic attempt to find, and define, the meaning of their lives.
headline: IN SHORT/SMALL PRESSES: FICTION

title: Eco-Warriors
author: Rik Scarce
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: ECO-WARRIORS: Understanding the Radical Environmental Movement.  By Rik Scarce. (Noble Press, Paper, $11.95.) The direct-action wing of the environmental movement has garnered both widespread praise and opprobrium. An overwhelming groundswell of support transformed Greenpeace from a daring but ragtag band of eco-guerrillas into the largest environmental organization in the world in barely over a decade. Yet last spring's bombing incident in Oakland, Calif., involving two organizers of the group Earth First! exposed an underlying bias in the news media. Despite strong evidence to the contrary, many reporters unquestioningly accepted police and Federal Bureau of Investigation charges that the two activists had themselves planted the device. In "Eco-Warriors" the journalist Rik Scarce examines the controversial world of radical environmentalism, providing a sympathetic and fascinating look inside the hearts and minds of those who would meld Gandhi with King Ludd. Much of the book is devoted to Earth First!, the best known of the dozen or so direct-action groups now operating around the world. Mr. Scarce charts the rise of the group, from its founding in 1980 by a quintet of wilderness advocates fed up with Secretary of the Interior James Watt's prodevelopment "sagebrush rebellion" and the increasing bureaucratization of the country's leading conservation groups. The author also details the arguments over tactics, strategies and goals that have begun to splinter the group, arguments reminiscent of those that divided the New Left. In addition, the blow-by-blow accounts of assorted acts of sabotage in defense of the environment by the Sea Shepherds and animal liberationists make intriguing, if sometimes disturbing, reading. Mr. Scarce occasionally weakens his superb reporting with superficial analysis, but on the whole this is a fine account for anyone looking for insight into the global environmental movement.

This odd little memoir of Djuna Barnes (1892-1982) has its curiosities and its charms. At once admiring of and admonitory toward its subject, the book serves as a loopy chronicle of the three-year friendship that developed between the aging, infirm and still piously eccentric poet and novelist and Hank O'Neal, a record producer and writer, who got to know Barnes after being asked to look in on her by their mutual friend, the photographer Berenice Abbott. Mr. O'Neal met Barnes late in 1978; by then the creator of the highly stylized novel "Nightwood" had been in virtual hiding in a one-room Greenwich Village apartment for nearly 40 years. Mr. O'Neal served as confidant, accountant, literary executor and errand boy to "an extraordinarily bright woman who lived in a time warp." Barnes, nearly 90, told him: "Don't think for a minute this is the real Djuna Barnes. The real Djuna Barnes is dead." What emerges from " 'Life Is Painful, Nasty & Short . . . In My Case It Has Only Been Painful & Nasty' " is a portrait of the writer in her final decline: proud, bowed and -- as Mr. O'Neal and others before him who had befriended her were forced to conclude -- insufferable.

author: Jonathan Sternfield
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE LOOK OF HORROR: Scary Moments From Scary Movies.  By Jonathan Sternfield. (Courage Books/Running Press, $14.98.) Covering a genre of movies that runs from "The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari" to "Little Shop of Horrors," "The Look of Horror" is a compressed history that is long on images and short on words, a well-illustrated, smartly written recap of some of the more frightening moments in movie history -- and the faces that make those moments memorable. This is a fan's book and never pretends to be a groundbreaking study of horror films. No long-winded theories or footnotes about What It All Means, just page after page of the bright, fantastic visions from the classics we know so well (and some we may have forgotten). Jonathan Sternfield, a freelance writer and photographer, breaks his study into different sections, covering aliens, creatures, ghosts and the demons among us -- the bad seeds, the ordinary people who can be the most terrifying monsters around. The author wisely keeps his opinions short, crisp and to the point. His text amounts to plot summaries and critical commentaries on the quality of the films. What animates this book are the photos of these scary monsters and super freaks. Mr. Sternfield has some interesting inclusions: in a book rife with werewolves, blobs and tarantulas the size of 747's, for example, he has included "Fatal Attraction" as a horror film for a new generation. We cover the gamut here, from monsters alien and otherwise to seemingly innocent demonic devices (the car in John Carpenter's "Christine," the red-headed doll in "Child's Play"). Mr. Sternfield delivers what he promises and does it in a loose, readable style. And the coffeetable format makes it effective; the pictures are large and lurid -- the better to frighten you with, my dear.

author: Madge Bellamy
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: A DARLING OF THE TWENTIES.  By Madge Bellamy. (Vestal, Paper, $19.95.) Although her name is now generally unknown, Madge Bellamy was a star of the silent screen. While most of her 57 movies may have been mediocre, and many remain hard to locate or lost forever, a handful possess cult interest, such as "Lorna Doone" or "The Iron Horse," which was directed by John Ford. (At the height of her popularity, fans could purchase a "Lorna Doone" cape and a Madge Bellamy cap.) Though she tried to shed an ingenue image and to negotiate the transition into talking pictures, Bellamy never really accomplished either. In her lavishly illustrated memoir, "A Darling of the Twenties," completed before her death in January (when she was probably 90 years old), Bellamy wants desperately to understand and explain what she calls her "Cinderella story in reverse." But in trying to account for a crucial moment when she turned down the lead in "The Trial of Mary Dugan," Bellamy exclaims, "Why did I do this? A thousand sleepless nights haven't solved the puzzle for me." In one embarrassing passage after the other, Bellamy betrays the naivete that apparently retarded both her career and her personal development. She says more than once, "I wish that I had gone to a psychiatrist, but I never did." Bellamy lived out most of the second half of her pathetic life "in abject poverty" with her "stage and screen identity undisclosed," and she last captured headlines for a few days in 1943, when she took a gun to a longtime companion, the lumber magnate A. Stanwood Murphy, after he abruptly married another woman. As the film historian Kevin Brownlow writes in his introduction, this poignant autobiography is "the dramatic and touching case history" of one of Hollywood's "victims." Whatever else it has to tell us about the shabby methods of the silent film industry, it inadvertently demonstrates that the firmament is fickle and that some stars are a lot less immortal than they may at first appear.

author: Devon Jersild
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: LOOKING FOR HOME: Women Writing About Exile. Edited by Deborah Keenan and Roseann Lloyd. (Milkweed Editions, Paper, $11.95.) Women have often used the metaphor of exile to describe their position at the margins of our culture. Those wishing to enter the American mainstream frequently feel divided between traditionally female values and the male-defined values of the marketplace; they struggle to shape the culture they enter, rather than be shaped by it. Given this context, we can doubly welcome the publication of "Looking for Home: Women Writing About Exile," an anthology of poetry written by women of diverse backgrounds, all with different definitions of alienation. Some of the poems describe the experience of learning a new language; some present women who want to hoard the words of their native tongue, to keep them safe, as Meredith Stricker writes, "against the enemy's decoding." There are poems about migration, the pulls of conflicting allegiances, the weight of history and the search for a unified self. Others tell stories of economic deprivation, chemical dependency and illness, of life as a lesbian in a culture hostile to sexual nonconformity. The collection includes work by poets as familiar as Sharon Olds and Denise Levertov, as well as poems by unknown writers. Its principle of organization remains somewhat obscure -- it is divided into seven sections with elusive quotations as titles, and even within one section two poems from one writer may or may not be placed together. Yet the anthology richly communicates both the singularity and the universality of women's deepest concerns. The poems that the editors, Deborah Keenan and Roseann Lloyd, have chosen may be more or less sophisticated in their technique, but they rarely strike a false note, and in most of them one hears language freighted with experience, the real voices of real women.

title: Step Right Up! The Adventure Of Circus In America
author: Arnold Aronson
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: For many people, including too many historians of popular culture, the modern American circus means Ringling Brothers and Barnum & Bailey and little else. STEP RIGHT UP! The Adventure of Circus in America (Betterway Publications, Cloth, $29.95; Paper, $19.95) goes a long way toward correcting that misconception. It celebrates the renaissance of the circus during the last decade and lovingly salutes the tenacious entrepreneurs who have held on through adversity over generations. Tent shows take center ring here and names like Circus Vargas, Clyde Beatty-Cole Brothers, Carson & Barnes, Franzen Brothers and Kelly-Miller are spotlighted, as well as such new wave productions as the Pickle Family Circus, the Big Apple Circus and Canada's Cirque du Soleil. The authors, LaVahn G. Hoh, a professor of drama at the University of Virginia, and William H. Rough, an independent scholar, are circus buffs who relish the details of how the shows move from town to town, how the performers and crews get fed and the minutiae of circus finance. Many of the more than 300 illustrations are unusual for a circus book -- details of decaying circus wagons or close-ups of the bale ring used to hoist a tent. This is an intimate and folksy book: managers and roustabouts are called by their first names and readers are made privy to their various physical ailments and financial reversals. "Step Right Up!" is also the first general study of the circus to examine in any detail the history of black and female performers. Unfortunately, the authors' style undermines the book. Early on they state, "We are not historians," and their writing confirms this. The tortured prose, erratic footnoting, absurd generalizations ("No one played music in colonial America"; "the total collapse of known civilization at the end of the Roman Empire") and especially the silly pop psychology that substitutes for cogent analysis cry out for excision at every turn. Nonetheless, the authors' unabashed love of the circus is contagious and the glimpses behind the scenes will delight circus enthusiasts.

author: Judith M Labelle

pull_quote: GREENWAYS FOR AMERICA.  By Charles E. Little. (Johns Hopkins University, $22.95.) Our system of land use may have lost much of its legitimacy and the planning profession may have few new ideas to offer, but Charles E. Little sees greenways as a grass-roots source of positive change. Greenways are protected natural areas; most are used for recreation such as hiking or biking, although some are designed primarily to protect environmental resources. Central to the greenway concept is the idea of linkage: creating connections among recreational resources, natural resources and communities. Mr. Little, whose previous books include "Challenge of the Land" and "Green Fields Forever," sees such networks as providing the framework for regional planning. "Greenways for America" makes clear that greenways have provided recreation, environmental enhancement, economic stimulus and civic pride in widely varied situations. Mr. Little concludes that to make a greenway is to make a community. The projects that the author visited are located across the country, from the San Juan Islands in Washington to the Hudson River Valley, and are "as rich and diverse as human ingenuity and topographic opportunity could make them." Mr. Little is an enthusiastic journalist with both an eye and an ear for local history and politics. With a few colorful strokes he brings to life the unconventional people he met along the way. The jumbo coffeetable book of the season must surely be the revised Baby Elephant Folio of AUDUBON'S BIRDS OF AMERICA (Abbeville, $185), which weighs in at 13 pounds. The original, of course, was the far heftier Double-Elephant Folio -- 435 color plates that John James Audubon painted between 1827 and 1838 in 200 sets, each weighing 56 pounds and priced, at one time, at $1,000. No longer! At Sotheby's last year a broken-up set was sold at auction for nearly $4 million. The present volume is a revised version of the edition Abbeville Press published in 1981 and dubbed the Baby Elephant Folio.

The editors had made a number of changes from the Double-Elephant -- in size, of course, halving the dimensions of the plates, and also in rearranging their order. In the original the plates appeared in the order in which Audubon painted them: six pages of warblers and cuckoos separating the male turkey and the female. In the Baby Elephant the plates have been reordered phylogenetically (that is, from the most primitive to the most highly evolved), which is the way standard bird guides are arranged. The present volume incorporates these changes and more -- bird names have been brought up to date (the Baltimore oriole is now, alas, the northern oriole), and so have the data that described the plates.

title: Words With Power
author: Northrop Frye
outlet: The New York Times
pull_quote: Words With Power Being a Second Study of "The Bible and Literature" By Northrop Frye 342 pages. Harcourt Brace Jovanovich. $24.95.   In his new book, "Words With Power," the distinguished literary theorist Northrop Frye examines the role of myth and metaphor in the Bible, showing how many of its central themes and images reverberate throughout Western literature. His conclusion is that "the organizing structures of the Bible and the corresponding structures of 'secular' literature reflect each other," that a finite number of species of myths (including myths of creation, fall, exodus, destruction and redemption) provide the narrative sources of literature.    Such ideas, of course, have been suggested by Mr. Frye before -- most notably in his famous 1957 study, "Anatomy of Criticism." In fact, "Words With Power" serves as both a sequel to his earlier study of the Bible and literature, "The Great Code: The Bible and Literature" (1982), and as a summing up and restatement of his overall critical views. As a result, some of this book (particularly its theoretical first half, which deals with different idioms of linguistic expression and the social function of literature) feels turgid and overly pedantic, as though Mr. Frye were simply reworking earlier assertions, while trying to answer questions raised by other critics.      It is the second part of the book, which actually deals with specific myths and archetypes found in the Bible (and their reinvention in modern Western literature), that will be most accessible to the nonspecialized public that Mr. Frye says he hopes to reach. Clearly the reader may question his methodology in this section: Mr. Frye's choice of examples is highly selective, sometimes even random, and his discussions of individual works can feel similarly arbitrary. In addition, many of his observations relating biblical stories to classical and primitive myths will be familiar to readers of Robert Graves's "White Goddess," James George Frazer's "Golden Bough" and Joseph Campbell's studies of mythology.   Still, this portion of "Words With Power" intermittently makes for lively and provocative reading. Drawing on his vast reading, Mr. Frye helps the reader recognize some of the recurring myths that connect religious and secular literature, and he shows how ideological and social changes can cause changes in the interpretation and emphasis of those myths. While early hard-line Christians regarded parallel classical myths as "demonic parodies of the true biblical ones," he adds that later, more liberal Christians came to regard classical mythology as a kind of "supplement or counterpoint to the Christian one."      As Mr. Frye sees it, the idea of the axis mundi -- the vertical line postulated by the ancients as running through the cosmos, connecting heaven to earth and earth to hell -- underlies many of Western literature's central myths, providing writers with a wealth of metaphors and images. Those images, he notes, tend to fall into two categories: ascent and descent. Images of ascent, which symbolize man's longing for heavenly perfection, include Jacob's ladder, the purgatorial mountain in Dante's "Divine Comedy," the turning staircase in T. S. Eliot's "Ash Wednesday" and the towers and spirals that recur in Yeats's poetry.    The reverse movement -- downward into death or damnation -- has yielded equally powerful images. Christ's descent to earth echoes Adam's fall from innocence, while Adam's expulsion from the garden is mirrored by the exile of Cain. Whereas Mr. Frye sees downward movements in Dante and Milton as "simply descents to death and hell," he argues that they can take on more creative aspects in other writers's work.   Proserpine's descent every winter into the nether world is a necessary prelude to her ascent in the spring -- and the earth's renewed fertility. Prometheus is punished by Zeus for bringing fire down from heaven but is heralded as the liberator of mankind. Ahab descends into madness as he searches for the great white whale but in doing so becomes a symbol of man's eternal quest for wisdom.      For Mr. Frye, the lower depths represent not only death or hell; they can also stand for "whatever in human nature is subordinated in the traditional structures." In Freud, this comes to signify the unconscious promptings of the id; in Marx, the energetic strivings of the proletariat. For such revolutionary thinkers, Mr. Frye says, "the initiative comes from below" and "the response to it is normally a journey of exploration downward."    In the course of "Words With Power," Mr. Frye also discusses other recurrent literary themes, like the wheel of fortune (which brings together images of ascent and descent into an endless cycle), the "purgatorial vision" of Exodus (a three-part narrative that moves from the bondage in Egypt to the wandering in the wilderness to the entry into the Promised Land), the Virgin Birth and the Garden of Eden.    His discussions of these themes, like the ones noted above, tend to be discursive, peremptory and quite often reductive. Darwin, Schopenhauer, Kierkegaard as well as Marx and Freud are dealt with in a couple paragraphs, and Blake's idiosyncratic mythology (once the subject of an entire book by Mr. Frye) is summarized in several pages. As a result, the reader finishes this volume hungry for more details and deeper analysis. Indeed, one can only surmise that that was one of Mr. Frye's objectives in writing "Words With Power" -- to send the reader back to other books, to other volumes of criticism, as well as to the Bible and other works of literature.

Ever since Methuselah exhibited his remarkable longevity, we have strained every scientific nerve to edge closer to his record. Yet our youth-smitten society frequently regards getting old as something rather gauche. Worse still, a growing number of graying citizens seem to concur. Fortunately, there are dissenting views, and seldom have they been expounded more persuasively -- and engagingly -- than in this sampler of Eda LeShan's syndicated "Life Over Sixty" columns. As hinted in the title, "It's Better to Be Over the Hill Than Under It," Ms. LeShan, a sixtysomething wife, mother and child psychologist, sees our elongated life spans less as a problem than as a privilege, at least considering the alternative. The overall message is that even if after 60 some of the best may be behind us, what's left can be pretty good. She introduces us to a 92-year-old man who has trouble finding chess partners because he beats the pants off most of them. And there are the childhood sweethearts who went their different ways, only to rekindle their romance -- after the age of 90. This book is no starry-eyed paean to the "golden years." All Ms. LeShan offers is a guide to turning what Cicero called "our play's last act" into a thing that merits some applause.

Composed with wit and economy, "The Effigy" is a slim collection of eight sharply observed vignettes, many suffused with undertones of rue. In the title story, an illiterate widow gains enough of a sense of selfhood by learning to read that she is finally free to act out her long-suppressed resentment of the husband she dutifully mourns. In "Custody," the narrator's wife, a compulsive dieter, "scarcely dents the bed, leaves little ripples where I make large waves. . . . Her body has no hair, her hair no body." At his daughter's wedding, his sense of loss is acute: "Flick off fathering in a mere ceremony? Caring is not as hard as pretending not to." Leo, the shoe salesman in "Where Touching Is a Talent," lives for the Thursday nights he spends at Roseland. He married Sophie because she "talked only when Leo wanted . . . and never while dancing, as reverent as in temple. A scented hanky soaked up the sweat of their palms and her breath was Wrigley's sweet." But Sophie lost interest in the rest of life when she failed to conceive a child: "her spirit ran out with her monthly flow." In contrast, Renie Dugan in "Equations" has been engaged for 12 years to a vacillating lover. "Her trousseau saw her through every vagary of fashion, from mini to midcalf to midknee. . . . the hems going up and down with her hopes." But when her engagement ring drops through the drain in the sink, she lets herself "slip from its noose." The hallmark of this gifted writer's prose is the trenchant phrase that uses few words to suggest whole paragraphs. Not all of Joan Millman's stories are of equal quality, but their stylistic flair makes her first collection of stories a pleasure to read.

A substantial and extensively illustrated monograph, with thoughtful essays by the art historian Robert Rosenblum and Andy Grundberg, a photography critic for The New York Times, MIKE AND DOUG STARN (Abrams, $39.95) attempts to establish the two brothers as historically significant artists. The Starn Twins, as they are commonly known, first appeared on the art scene in the late 80's and have yet to reach their 30th birthdays. The speed with which they are being inserted into the history books is typical of today's art world; that two 

photographers 

could achieve such notoriety reflects that neglected medium's progress toward artistic legitimacy. The Starns first impressed audiences with a salon-style installation at the 1987 Biennial at the Whitney Museum of American Art, New York City's prominent showcase for new talent. Large and small works, including a double self-portrait, were artfully arranged on two walls in a corner of the gallery. The brothers introduced a method that they have continued to develop ever since and that is well documented in the book: negatives are scored and pockmarked, prints are stained with various off-color washes and the traditionally inviolate print is torn, cut up and reassembled with adhesive tape. The Starns also reinserted emotionally loaded subject matter into art -- Christ figures, historical martyrs such as Anne Frank and Martin Luther King Jr. -- rejecting post-modernism's ironic distance. Their work struck a chord with many, while others dismissed it as sentimental and reactionary. The Starns receive high praise from Mr. Grundberg and from Mr. Rosenblum, who declares that their work "is becoming unexpectedly central to the history of contemporary art." However, with only a few years of full-time professional production to their credit, such an evaluation seems premature.

Since we have heard little else about him these last few years, there is a tendency to view Bo Jackson as living the athletically charmed American life: a versatile athlete, a standout at Auburn University, a Heisman Trophy winner, husband, father, hitter of tape-measure home runs, able to leap tall obstacles with a single bound. "Bo Knows Bo," Mr. Jackson's autobiography (written with the sports journalist Dick Schaap), gives a personal view of this man with many helmets. Growing up black in the South presented challenges that athletics could not answer; not everything in Mr. Jackson's life has been sweetness, light and Nike endorsements. This affecting and brightly written memoir tells us that Vincent Edward Jackson, born in 1962 in Alabama, had an angry, tempestuous spirit. As a child he was called "Bo'-hog," soon shortened to Bo; he was a bully who could steal anything from lunch money to bicycles but "couldn't steal a father." Mr. Jackson speaks with savvy eloquence and is refreshingly matter-of-fact. For example, he says that "too many athletes allow colleges to mislead them. . . . It takes the dignity out of college athletics when you have a guy playing football who can't spell football." Clearly and guilelessly, he gives a rueful, heartfelt message about children. title: The Best American Essays 1990
author: Justin Kaplan
outlet: The New York Times Book Review

It is hard to imagine any essay published last year more moving than Natalie Kusz's account of being mauled by a dog at the age of 7, or as grotesquely hilarious as Ann Hodgman's description in Spy magazine of taste-testing different brands of dog food, or as insightful as Stephen Jay Gould's examination of the origins of baseball -- which somehow comes to be a commentary on the abortion debate. The biographer Justin Kaplan and Robert Atwan, the editor of the "Best American Essays" series, have brought together 21 distinctive essays that make fair claim to being the year's best. Choosing, Mr. Atwan says, "public, rather than personal, essays" by writers who "move between the topical requirements of an article and the literary demands of an essay" -- or, as Mr. Kaplan puts it, "between stunt flying and scheduled air traffic" -- the editors have achieved an eclectic blend of the solemn and the laid-back, the incisive and the discursive. Here we have Joseph Epstein on the value of envy, Sue Hubbell on Elvis sightings in Kalamazoo, Leonard Michaels on the "R" word (relationships), Michael Pollan on lawn care -- or, rather, lawn neglect. Mr. Kaplan and Mr. Atwan have found writers with a gift for the memorable phrase ("My existence," says Anatole Broyard after learning he has cancer of the prostate, "had taken on a kind of meter, as in poetry, or in taxis") and for the memorable incident: Stanley Elkin describing his meeting with Hubert Humphrey, Randy Shilts describing a roomful of uneaten salads. Probably the hallmark entry in the book is the final one, Tom Wolfe's piece for Harper's on the American novel, which Mr. Kaplan describes as "surely one of the noisier literary events of 1989." Provocative, self-serving, eminently refutable (printed here, unfortunately, without the letters Harper's received in response), Mr. Wolfe's is a piece that can best be described as effective. As all these essays are, each in its own way.

Out on the street, in parks or on sidewalks, children have displayed immense resourcefulness in their determination to have fun. Amanda Dargan, director of folk arts at the Queens Council on the Arts, and Steven Zeitlin, director of City Lore, a New York cultural studies group, hurtle "the triviality barrier" as they detail various aspects of city play, from the historical -- kite flying below 14th Street was illegal by the mid-19th century -- to the ridiculous -- early 20th-century reformers once gave bowling a 77.1 percent ranking on a wholesomeness scale. The pictures, by Martha Cooper, Arthur Leipzig and dozens of other photographers, are the main attraction here. Their black-and-white brilliance shows more than a century of exuberant children riding homemade go-carts, raising pigeons, jumping rope and unleashing fire hydrants. A block at a time, a stoop at a time, a face at a time, several generations of artists and photographers have captured a startling diversity of children and amusements, documenting the street as both playground and "test kitchen for new urban cultural forms." New York is such a grown-up place that sometimes we forget children are just as goal-oriented as adults. The goal is fun. "City Play" is both reminder and suggestion. Checkers, anyone?
headline: The City as Game Board

Beginning with "Crazy Ladies," in which an 11-year-old boy's encounter with a locally renowned eccentric illuminates the puzzling changes overtaking his seemingly conventional family, the author establishes an elegiac tone that carries throughout the entire volume.  Many of the stories in "Distant Friends" are retrospective looks at unsettling, even brutal, childhood experiences. An outstanding example is "The Burning," which opens with an adult narrator recalling himself as a 10-year-old boy -- in a hospital bed recovering from numerous broken bones, his face "so swollen with bruises that it resembles an overripe plum." The narrator traces the events leading up to his battering, citing his father's progressive detachment from the family as an early omen. "There was no particular, unmistakable sign," he recalls, "just a gradual change in the atmosphere -- the way the air will seem to thicken, and even become eerily visible, as a prelude to bad weather." While such inchoate understanding of the dangers of the adult world is typical of all the young protagonists in these stories, not all the book's children appear as wounded innocents. In "El Paso" and "Passion Play," for example, they assume the role of protector, yet in both stories they are doomed in their attempts to shield those who are more vulnerable than themselves. Compassionate adults also pay a price, as in "Wildfires," the story of the wife of a Vietnam veteran who loses herself to her husband's suffering. In the final story, which tells of a man's aborted effort to comfort friends whose child has died, Greg Johnson crystallizes his grim but affecting vision with the ironic suggestion that the closest friends may in fact be those who manage to stay at arm's length.

title: The Man Who Changed The World
author: Mikhail S Gorbachev
outlet: The New York Times
pull_quote: The Man Who Changed the World  The Lives of Mikhail S. Gorbachev  By Gail Sheehy  Illustrated. 401 pages. HarperCollins . $22.95.    Gail Sheehy promises much in "The Man Who Changed the World," a biography of Mikhail S. Gorbachev that grew out of a portrait of the Soviet leader that Ms. Sheehy wrote for Vanity Fair magazine.   Taking off from the perception widely held in the Soviet Union that there are many sides to her subject's character, Ms. Sheehy subtitles her book "The Lives of Mikhail S. Gorbachev" and formulates a theory of his "incarnations" based on one of her previous books.   "The theory in my book 'Passages,' " she writes, "is that each of us develops throughout adulthood by stages. Between each stage are points of decision between progress and regression where we are challenged to shed a protective structure, and when we do we are left exposed and vulnerable, capable of stretching in ways we hadn't known before. For exceptional individuals, like Gorbachev, such passages assume the dimensions of deep personal transformations -- they become in some ways different people."      She hints ominously about one of these sides of Mr. Gorbachev when in the third paragraph of her text she quotes a former senior Soviet analyst for the State Department who has studied Mr. Gorbachev for a decade: "I think he's capable of a great cruelty."    But Ms. Sheehy delivers somewhat less than she promises. Her idea of cruelty is summed up in a remembrance by Andrei Brezhnev, who describes his grandfather, Leonid, taking pleasure in keeping pigeons and doves and hitting their cage to see them all fly around, terrified. This seems mild compared with Nikita S. Khrushchev's purported adolescent penchant for bashing cats' heads against stone walls, not to speak of Stalin's unspeakable sadism. As examples of Mr. Gorbachev's cruelty Ms. Sheehy offers us no detail. Nothing.   As for his multiple "lives," she tells us little more than what is surely self-evident to any reader, namely that Mr. Gorbachev is mercurial, intuitive, adaptable, capable of walking a tightrope and turning on a dime, and no longer in control of the revolution he began.     It is too bad that Ms. Sheehy lets her readers down so, because despite all its huffing and puffing her book is enlightening in many ways. She never got to interview Mr. Gorbachev himself, but she did manage to visit his home village, Privolnoye, and to pick up a trail of his friends and associates that led from the girl next door right to the top of his Government command.   From these contacts she has learned much about Mr. Gorbachev's family background: that his ancestors were Cossacks who "had pushed down from the Ukraine and the Don area in search of virgin soil and religious freedom, settling in the southernmost wilds of the territory of Stavropol known as the Caucasus"; that the women in his family were strong and outspoken; that his maternal grandfather, the family patriarch during Mr. Gorbachev's childhood, was chairman of the local collective farm, or kolkhoz, which made him the most important person in the village; and that by contrast his paternal grandfather was arrested and deported to Archangel in 1937, purportedly for having hidden 40 pounds of grain for his family from the collective's harvest.     From this background Ms. Sheehy draws plausible enough conclusions: that the strong women around him in his childhood explains why Mr. Gorbachev concedes so much power to his wife, Raisa, who has even been his instructor at times and whom he regards as a full partner, referring to her as "my General." And that the conflicting roles that his grandfathers played -- with one participating in Stalin's regime and the other becoming its victim -- account for the division in Mr. Gorbachev's character that allowed him to rise to the top of the ruling establishment and then to turn around and destroy it.   Unfortunately, she too often trivializes these perceptions with the style in which she presents them. Writing of Mr. Gorbachev's youth as if she were there present to observe it, she intones: "Driving the harvester every day, choking in the sworls of dust from the steppe, sweat streaming from his face, a continual trilling in his ears, he worked like a demon and waited for the Party to take notice." Characters variously "gush," "squeal" and "rhapsodize" where it would have perfectly adequately served for them simply to "say." At one point, she describes Mr. Gorbachev as "a brilliant chameleon," which seems an inapt way of saying what she is trying to convey, namely that Gorbachev is cleverly adaptable.     But the book's biggest shortcoming is its failure to dramatize Mr. Gorbachev's changes. Though she titles her various sections "First Gorbachev: Country Cossack 1931-1949," "Second Gorbachev: First-Generation Apparatchik 1950-1977" and so forth through "Sixth Gorbachev: Red Star Falling Spring 1990," she is only able to convey the startling contrast between Mr. Gorbachev as a genius on the world stage and Mr. Gorbachev as a failure at home.   What his problem finally comes down to, at least in Ms. Sheehy's view, is that despite the halting moves he has made toward a market economy, Mr. Gorbachev at heart still believes in socialism. As she quotes the image of a cabbage used by the writer Olas Adamovich: "Gorbachev believes that if he takes off the decayed leaves there will be a healthy cabbage inside. The apparatchiks know it's dangerous to strip off the leaves, because it's rotten inside, it will all have to be thrown away. Gorbachev is the last romantic socialist."   The wonder of Ms. Sheehy's book is that it goes through such a complicated dance to make such a simple point.
headline: Books of The Times; Gorbachev the Man, or Maybe Men

title: Love And Its Place In Nature
author: Jonathan Lear
outlet: The New York Times
pull_quote: Love and Its Place in Nature  A Philosophical Interpretation of Freudian Psychoanalysis  By Jonathan Lear  243 pages. Farrar, Straus & Giroux . $18.95.    It is commonly thought that in a typical psychoanalysis, the analyst eventually discovers, perhaps through a reported dream or a slip of the tongue, what is troubling the unconscious mind of the analysand. The analyst then announces the new-found insight and brings the patient in a single leap to the mountaintop of understanding. Eureka! The sufferer has been cured.   But those who have actually been through analysis report that it is a slow and tortuous process, more like climbing a mountain a few inches at a time, with each tiny step gaining a vantage point to see just a little farther.    In his profound new book, "Love and Its Place in Nature: A Philosophic Interpretation of Freudian Psychoanalysis," Jonathan Lear reveals that, surprisingly enough, early in his career, Sigmund Freud held a modified version of the former view. In his deep commitment to a 19th-century scientistic interpretation of the new discipline he was evolving, he believed that hysterics expelled the "foreign bodies" of their traumatic memories in a process of catharsis that resembled some law of thermodynamics.   It was only later and gradually that he came to understand that some primitive form of mental functioning underlay conscious thought and that it could only be coaxed to the surface gradually by an interpretation just one step ahead of the patient's understanding, not shouted down from the mountaintop, as it were. Moreover, the process of bringing the material to the surface involved not a strictly scientific procedure, but instead a form of love.   What Mr. Lear sees in these discoveries is a revolution that went much further than even Freud himself anticipated. In Mr. Lear's words, this revolution "contained three related elements whose significance we have only begun to understand: a science of subjectivity; the discovery of an archaic form of mental functioning; the positing of Love as a basic force in nature." He adds: "To take these ideas seriously would be to view the world very differently than we do now." In "Love and Its Place in Nature," he strives for that altered world view.   It is not a simple book to read. Aside from being a clinical associate of the Western New England Institute for Psychoanalysis, the author is a professor of philosophy at Yale University and the author of "Aristotle: The Desire to Understand" and "Aristotle and Logical Theory." His thesis is so closely reasoned and rigorously worded that in a footnote in Chapter VI he feels compelled to remind us that "I began to discuss the distinction between accepting responsibility and holding responsible in Chapter II," as if his readers can't be expected to remember what they have already read.   The author sticks closely to Freud's own writing, so that his development of the master's ideas is done in the context of such works as "Studies in Hysteria," "The Interpretation of Dreams," "The Ego and the Id," "Beyond the Pleasure Principle" and "Civilization and Its Discontents," as well as many of Freud's less familiar works. Not incidentally, following a suggestion made by Bruno Bettelheim in his book "Freud and Man's Soul" (Knopf, 1983), he substitutes the words "I" and "it" for "ego" and "id," so that Freud's most famous statement reads "Where It was, there I shall become."    He explores the philosophical implications of psychoanalysis and compares his conclusions with those of thinkers like Kant and Nietzsche, finding both of them, and others, disappointingly limited in their views of the mind. In general he blames modern philosophy for its "tendency to investigate the structure of the human soul in isolation from any consideration of how that structure came about."    But a careful reading of "Love and Its Place in Nature" yields valuable rewards. He makes one understand how psychoanalysis works not only on the therapist's couch but also as a condition of being alive. He writes: "Psychoanalysis, Freud once said, is a cure through love. On the manifest level, Freud meant that psychoanalytic therapy requires the analysand's emotional engagement with the analyst and the analyst's empathic understanding of his patient. But the latent content of this remark, which Freud only gradually discovered, and then through a glass darkly, is that psychoanalysis in its essence promotes individuation. In that sense, psychoanalysis is itself a manifestation of love. And the emergence of psychoanalysis onto the human scene must, from this perspective, be part of love's developmental history."   Is psychoanalysis dying as a practical therapy? Mr. Lear asks in his Introduction. And answers: "To my mind, the issue is not whether psychoanalysis is obsolete, but whether the individual is." For all their immense value in relieving human suffering, he writes, "there is no evidence that drugs, surgery or electroconvulsive therapy can treat more than the grossest of psychic phenomena. That there will be marvelous advances in neurology and pharmacology is beyond question; that they will solve the conflicts inherent in living    this    particular life is fantasy."   He goes on: "And however valuable it may be to jump-start someone out of a depression, from the point of view of our commitment to the individual, the all-important question is: what happens next? Does the person use the relief from crippling pain as an opportunity to work through the meanings and conflicts inherent in his life; or is he 'relieved' of that opportunity? This is ultimately the question of whether a person is freed    to    become an individual -- or 'freed'    from    that possibility."   Mr. Lear disdains self-help books, because "selves are not that easy to help." He adds, "An individual requires a kind of nurturing and growth that goes far beyond aerobics and quick-fix therapy." Yet "Love and Its Place in Nature" may be the ultimate self-help book. It not only offers a form of spiritual nutriment for the self, it also defines that self with a clear profundity that few readers will have encountered before.
headline: Books of The Times; Psychoanalysis as a Step in the Evolution of Love

title: Road Song
author: Natalie Kusz.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: ROAD SONG  By Natalie Kusz. 258 pp. New York: Farrar, Straus & Giroux. $18.95.    THE author of this memoir has suffered so much in her 27 years that writing about it involved a risk. "Road Song" could have been a saccharine tract about the triumph of the human spirit or such a painful tale that even reading it would hurt. Instead it's a calm, reflective affirmation of family love.   Natalie Kusz was 6 years old when her parents moved with their four children from Los Angeles to Alaska, pursuing the dream of a freer life. For years her Polish-born father had told his wife and children about the woods he'd known as a boy, until his longing to get back to the land became theirs. "My mother, and then we all, had turned nostalgic for places we'd never seen, countries full of trees and cold rivers and neighbors far apart." In 1969 they sold their house and most of their belongings and headed north in their unreliable car, pulling a small trailer full of supplies.   On the trip, in keeping with family tradition, they harmonized on road songs -- " 'Wayfaring Stranger,' 'My Lord, I'm on My Journey,' and every Russian and Polish verse my father had ever taught us." The "true and unmuffled phrasings" blended and soared "until our very bones and their hollows resonated and increased with the joy of them." Music is as essential to the Kuszes as food. It gives voice to joy, consoles and even heals, seeing them through times that seem to go only from bad to worse.   The journey itself holds great promise. Away from big cities, the travelers encounter a "fresh sort of kindness" and make friends who share their dream. In Alaska, however, their money runs low, a brutal winter comes on and there are no jobs. Along with others in similar straits, they scrounge for food and warm clothing at the dump outside Fairbanks and camp on a river bank.   A relative helps them buy a piece of land, wild and remote and with no road in. Because it's too late in the year to build, they tack a makeshift room onto the trailer. By the time Ms. Kusz's father finds work as a carpenter, a job that takes him a long way from home, stove oil and groceries are all but gone. Waiting for his first paycheck to arrive, the family pawns its cherished musical instruments. Less intrepid people would cut their losses and leave, but the tougher the going gets, the tougher the Kuszes get too.   Then Natalie is attacked by a neighbor's sled dog (vicious because it's underfed) and injured so massively she's not expected to live. The attack costs her an eye and years of misery -- reconstructive surgery, infections, skin grafts that won't take and the attentions of "emotional sightseers," ghouls who want to hear every detail. Yet she insists that her family, especially her mother, suffered more. "The truth is, I think, that the casualties among us include not just those who are dying, or bleeding, or recovering from injury, but also the caretakers around the edges whose selves fall sacrificed to their charges."   More blows follow, including both parents' illnesses, the loss of a house that they manage to build and the medical horrors that Natalie endures. The family rallies again and again, sustained by friends, religious faith and rueful humor. "Someday," Natalie's mother tells her and her sisters, "some guy will say to you, 'Let's run away to the wilderness and live like pioneers. . . .' And you'll look back at that man and tell him, 'Get lost, buddy, I've done my time.' " Reality can vanquish romanticism, but not Natalie's spiritual sturdiness.   Ms. Kusz sings her own song of this tortuous road in a true voice, with no self-pity whatsoever. If her prose sometimes shades into lyrical overkill, becoming self-consciously biblical, its pitch is more often perfect. "Adversity," she observes, is "the small, hard seed of courage." Of all people, she ought to know.   Ms. Kusz took a college teaching job in Minnesota two years ago. She still gets lost easily driving around St. Paul, disoriented by freeways. To head true north to Alaska, where most of her family still lives, she needs no compass but her heart.
headline: 'Get Lost, Buddy, I've Done My Time'

title: The Man Who Thought He Was Messiah
author: Howard Mittelmark

pull_quote: THE MAN WHO THOUGHT HE WAS MESSIAH.  By Curt Leviant. (Jewish Publication Society, $18.95.) Hasidism appears profoundly conservative to modern eyes, but it was once a vibrant, radical, even revolutionary, movement. Breaking from the Judaism of the period, which they regarded as elitist, the Hasidic teachers of the 18th century sought to bring the gift of transcendence to the common man; through singing, dancing and fervent prayer, Hasidim aspired to mystical communion with God. Among the greatest of the Hasidic teachers was Rabbi Nachman of Bratslav, famous for the wisdom of his storytelling. In his enchanting, magical third novel, Curt Leviant becomes a modern Nachman and summons up a world suffused with a tangible spirituality, a world where trees or dreams or numbers might speak prophecy, where God is ever immanent behind the thin veil of the printed word. Sensual and intriguing, "The Man Who Thought He Was Messiah" shows us Reb Nachman in 1800, his incredibly eventful final year. It begins with God's whisper, a hint of Messianic destiny: Nachman might bring salvation to the scattered nation of Israel. Despite the presumption of this notion, Nachman seeks to prove himself worthy, but fails: he falls in love with Lizabeta, a young peasant "more beautiful than the alphabet." In fitting punishment, Nachman loses his ability to read; to atone for their liaison, he must leave Bratslav. Thus he travels to Vienna and studies composition with a proud but likable Beethoven; returning home with his new language of music, he finds his literacy partly restored. Setting out again, this time for the Holy Land, Nachman stops in Constantinople and, in a storybook scenario, cures the sultan's daughter of a storybook ailment. In Palestine divine tests await, and Nachman must probe his deepest values. Exquisitely written, Mr. Leviant's engaging exploration of the spirit will seduce and delight readers of any faith -- or lack thereof.
