title: The Distant Friend
author: Claude Roy
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE DISTANT FRIEND.  By Claude Roy. Translated by Hugh A. Harter. (Holmes & Meier, $19.95.) Although Claude Roy has published many volumes of fiction, poetry, essays and art criticism in his native France, little of his work has appeared in English translation. "The Distant Friend," then, will probably introduce Mr. Roy to most American readers. This slim novel, which was first published in France in 1987 and has now been ably translated by Hugh A. Harter, takes the form of a wandering, elegiac memoir. The narrator, Etienne, has lived a life of sacrifice and postponement. Confining himself to the family estate in the provinces, where he cares for his invalid mother and balances the accounts, Etienne doggedly accepts his solitude: "I was born a bachelor and would remain a bachelor." His greatest consolation lies in his friendship with Stefan Stein, a German Jewish refugee he first met when they were both teen-agers. Unlike Etienne, this doppelganger is rootless, polyglot and, by nature of his Jewish ancestry, positioned at the tragic center of 20th-century history. Their two destinies diverge rather quickly. While Etienne putters around the farm, Stefan flees France in 1939 for Argentina, becomes an eminent lawyer and writer and, 40 years later, finds his life threatened by Peronist thugs. According to Etienne, their friendship has taught him the "luxury of existing in the eyes of someone else through and for myself." Before long, however, this pairing of Etienne with his opposite number begins to feel like a literary contrivance, one the author has festooned with a string of cliches about politics, history and friendship. As an attempt, in Etienne's words, to preserve memories "suspended at the edge of the abyss of time where oblivion will swallow  [ them ]  up," "The Distant Friend" falls sadly short.    Engage    it is, engaging it isn't.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: Dazzle
author: Susan Dundon
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: DAZZLE.  By Judith Krantz. (Crown, $21.95.) Anyone who has ever read and drooled over a Judith Krantz novel -- or been forced to confess, "No, but I saw the mini-series" -- will not be disappointed in "Dazzle." Its scrumptious heroine, Jazz Kilkullen, is a brilliant photographer of celebrities, based in Venice, Calif. She is the daughter of a Swedish actress, Sylvie Norberg, and a rancher, Mike Kilkullen, to whom she has been completely devoted since her mother's death when Jazz was 8. Jazz works at Dazzle, the name of the studio she owns with her two partners, Mel and Pete, who specialize, respectively, in food and cars. Sharing the same space is the ever ambitious, avaricious Phoebe Milbank, their representative. An enviable number of men orbit around Jazz, who is a study in gold tones, with rich golden skin, golden brown hair and golden eyes. Jazz's admirers include Sam, an Australian actor whose unimaginable gorgeousness puts him at a painful social disadvantage, and a photojournalist named Gabriel, who first seduced Jazz when she was 18 -- by flicking his tongue over the tips of her eyelashes. Finally, there is the good guy, Casey Nelson, an investor turned cow boss, who works for Jazz's father at the family ranch, 100 square miles of coveted undeveloped coastal real estate between Los Angeles and San Diego. But the people who provide the true drama of "Dazzle" are those who plot to get the precious Kilkullen ranch sold off to developers: Mike's bitter, scheming first wife, Liddy, and Jazz's two half sisters, Valerie, a dry, sexless interior decorator, and the precocious Fernanda. The latter, having experienced her first orgasm at age 3, spends the next 36 years trying to find a lover as good as herself. I wouldn't dream of revealing how this search, or the struggle to save the ranch, ends. "Dazzle," if not perfectly dazzling, is appropriately entertaining. Closet Krantz enthusiasts will find that it fits nicely into the jacket of "Rabbit at Rest" and can be read comfortably on the train.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: Mexican Voices/American Dreams
author: Marilyn P Davis
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: MEXICAN VOICES/AMERICAN DREAMS: An Oral History of Mexican Immigration to the United States.  By Marilyn P. Davis. (Holt, $29.95.) This oral history follows a familiar format: numerous personal accounts arranged by topic, with short introductory sections by the author. Marilyn P. Davis, an independent scholar, draws on the experiences of a wide variety of Mexican immigrants (both legal and illegal), from field hands to professors, from those who stay only briefly in the United States to third-generation American citizens. Inevitably, the stories of immigrants who have adapted to life in    el norte    and have attained successful middle-class careers in this country are the least interesting and do not seem appreciably different from similar stories involving other immigrant groups. The portrayal of the broader Mexican experience, on the other hand, is fascinating. The economic motives for Mexican immigration to the United States are well known, but "Mexican Voices/American Dreams" shows that there are also deep cultural ramifications. For many Mexican children, stories about "over there" take on the aura of myth and exert a pull independent of economic necessity, so that immigration has become a rite of passage for Mexican youth. The separation of parents from children and husbands from wives -- often for years -- can devastate families, as some of Ms. Davis's most poignant pages show. An excellent chapter covers what is in effect an underground railroad for crossing into the United States; illegal immigration has become a major service industry along parts of the border. The book's major disappointment is that it lacks the lyric quality that characterizes the best oral histories. Nevertheless, "Mexican Voices/American Dreams" provides a welcome contrast to the depersonalization characteristic of some treatments of Mexican immigration, which all too often is considered only from the viewpoint of the American border patrol.
headline: IN SHORT: NONFICTION

title: Human Rights In Iraq
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: HUMAN RIGHTS IN IRAQ.  By Middle East Watch. (Human Rights Watch/Yale University, $19.95.) This cogent study offers grim details of the systematic repression of its citizens by the Iraqi Government over the last two decades of rule by the Baath Socialist Party and since 1979 by the regime of Saddam Hussein. During this period, according to "Human Rights in Iraq," the 16 million inhabitants of this oil-rich but troubled land have been subject to arbitrary arrest, imprisonment, torture, deportation, expulsion and execution. The often rebellious Kurdish minority (about 20 percent of the population) has suffered a crueler fate: thousands have been massacred, most recently by poison gas attacks, and some 500,000 have been resettled, no one is sure where, since the end of the Iran-Iraq war in 1988. These charges by Middle East Watch, a group that monitors human rights practices in the region, are based on witnesses' corroborated testimony and other research; all the charges have been denied by Baghdad. Although there appears to be no opposition to Saddam Hussein's regime outside the Kurdish areas -- those who conform are offered peace and prosperity -- the Government refuses to admit any human rights investigative body into the country. This study also examines how the United States has applied human rights criteria in its dealings with Iraq. Before Mr. Hussein's invasion of Kuwait, the record was not exemplary. Despite widely circulated State Department reports on Iraq's dismal record, this country offered financial aid and allowed exports of technology, some of it military, to the regime that now threatens the entire Middle East with bloodshed. Once known as the cradle of civilization, the Tigris-Euphrates valley has become a caldron of violence and terror.

The intense debate on the greenhouse effect and the prospect of global warming has conjured up doomsday visions of environmental upheaval in the next century. Taking exception to the "crisis psychology" of climate Cassandras, Louise B. Young has written a concerned but straightforward summary of the current state of scientific knowledge of such issues as greenhouse warming, acid rain and the depletion of the ozone layer. With a gift for rendering complex scientific issues in lucid language, she attempts in "Sowing the Wind" to put the climate controversy in perspective by describing what science has learned about the evolution of climate on the earth, as well as the effects of man's inadvertent meddling. Ms. Young, the author of "Earth's Aura," is very good at explaining how climate is generated by the miraculously intricate and subtle interplay among land, oceans and atmosphere. It is not surprising, as she notes, that even the most advanced computers cannot handle the vast number of calculations needed to simulate the atmosphere's complexity faithfully, or that we have not been monitoring changes in this mercurial medium long enough to predict climate trends with any certainty. At the same time, Ms. Young does not discount the very real threat of changes brewing in the weather of the next century. In her final chapter she offers suggestions about what can be done right now. Unfortunately, this is the least satisfying part of the book, since she tends to rely on her considerable talent for lyrical prose and on brisk generalizations rather than dealing in more than a cursory way with some serious questions raised by the specter of global warming.

author: Kate Braverman

pull_quote: SQUANDERING THE BLUE.  By Kate Braverman. (Fawcett Columbine, $18.95.) If, as they say, beauty is in the eye of the beholder, it stands to reason that horror, too, lurks deep within the optic nerve. How else to explain the lushly menacing imagery in the poet and novelist Kate Braverman's latest book? Never have the gaudy tropical flora of Los Angeles and Hawaii produced such gorgeously poisonous fruit. The stories in "Squandering the Blue," Ms. Braverman's first collection of short fiction, take place "on the border between death and the Mardi Gras," a sinister, forbidding and unpredictable region of the mind where even the leaves on the trees seem to wear camouflage and carry Uzis. Flowers are the color of "bruises, violence and disaster." A sunset metastasizes above the cliffs. The rain doesn't stop, it merely goes into remission. In the feverish imaginations of Ms. Braverman's characters -- many of them former or current substance abusers -- danger is everywhere, particularly in the mirror. If the book seems excessive at times, the characters' crazed outlooks and histrionic predicaments aren't the only cause. Ms. Braverman has a penchant for repetition: identical phrases recur in several stories, and in one 16-page stretch the word "blue" appears 85 times. While this is clearly designed to evoke the hysterical frame of mind of a woman on the verge of a nervous breakdown, it runs the risk of driving readers to distraction en route. Overall, though, the women in "Squandering the Blue" are fitting representatives of the walking wounded, tropical Cassandras with a taste for flashy destruction. Dancing hypnotically on the lip of the volcano, they pour florid language into the fire to create brief, spectacular moments of illumination.

author: James Hamilton
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: Anyone who remembers Arthur Rackham's classic illustrations as just treacly pictures of fairies is probably repressing the scarier aspects of childhood. Rackham's supernatural landscapes and their inhabitants enchant us with equal measures of grace and terror. For each rosebud princess, he drew a fearful wolf, witch or mountain peak. In ARTHUR RACKHAM: A Biography (Arcade/Little, Brown, $40; after Dec. 31, $45), the art historian James Hamilton suggests that the Stamford House garden, across the street from Rackham's childhood home, might have been the source of his fantastic arborial people and anthropomorphic trees. Unfortunately the biography, though conscientious and affectionate, gives more insight into Rackham's finances than his imagination. Partly this is due to Mr. Hamilton's effort to correct the view of Rackham as "some kind of busy little gnome, acquainted with the fairies." Born in London in 1867, Rackham supported himself first as a clerk in an insurance office, then as a magazine illustrator. He married a portrait painter and had one daughter. From 1905, when his illustrated edition of "Rip Van Winkle" was gobbled up by the public and the critics, until his death in 1939, Christmas wasn't Christmas without a new Rackham book. Among the more familiar are "Peter Pan in Kensington," "A Midsummer Night's Dream," "The Pied Piper of Hamelin" and fairy tales by Hans Christian Andersen and the Grimm brothers; perhaps the best loved is his last, "The Wind in the Willows," published in 1940. Mr. Hamilton's biography invites you to lose yourself among hundreds of pictures selected from Rackham's books.

title: A Forest Of Kings
author: L Elisabeth Beattie
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: A FOREST OF KINGS: The Untold Story of the Ancient Maya. By Linda Schele and David Freidel. (Morrow, $29.95.) A frenzy to learn more about the ancient Maya, whose culture flourished in the Yucatan 3,000 years ago and whose ancestors still thrive by the millions in Mexico, Guatemala, Belize and western Honduras, may soon supplant our habit of looking chiefly to other continents to study pre-Christian advanced civilizations. For the decoding of Mayan hieroglyphs has revealed the startlingly sophisticated and brutal history of this Mesoamerican culture, described in painstaking detail by Linda Schele, a professor of art at the University of Texas, Austin, and David Freidel, an archeologist who teaches at Southern Methodist University. They helped decipher the glyphs and cartouches that reverse previous notions concerning the Maya's peaceful nature and uncomplicated existence. According to the authors, the three-tiered Maya world, consisting of "the starry arch of heaven, the stony Middleworld of earth made to flower and bear fruit by the blood of kings, and the dark waters of the Underworld below," was "thought to be alive and imbued with sacred power, including the sky, which was represented by a great crocodilian monster. This Cosmic Monster made the rains when it shed its blood in supernatural counterpoint to the royal sacrifices on the earth below." Ms. Schele and Mr. Freidel describe how oral tradition preserved many Mayan beliefs originally recorded on perishable paper; they claim that Central American festivals and such practices as shamanism derive from this ancient heritage. "The genius of the Maya was expressed through the creation of new visions of power," they write. "They invented political symbols that transformed and coordinated such age-old institutions as the extended family, the village, the shaman, and the patriarch into the stuff of civilized life." Although "A Forest of Kings" is in places thick with dry verbiage, it is throughout rich in revelatory research.

pull_quote: THE ROSE THIEVES.  By Heidi Jon Schmidt. (Harcourt Brace Jovanovich, $18.95.) "When you had expression, you were safe at any speed," observes a young piano student in Heidi Jon Schmidt's first collection of stories. "You could turn pain to understanding like straw into gold." And in this book Ms. Schmidt effects just such alchemy. "The Rose Thieves" is a collection of pieces that reveal an intimate portrait of the storms and intermittent calms of a somewhat eccentric family living in rural Connecticut. If forced to name a central character, it would certainly be Kate, the eldest daughter of the Vanderwald family. For it is through Kate that readers meet her mother (volatile, passionate, dissatisfied with her life) and her father (a relentless optimist with a spent trust fund and an erratic income in futures trading), as well as her two sisters, Audie and Grace, the family peace-keepers. When a grown-up Kate reassures a friend that "love without difficulty could hardly be called love at all," she speaks from experience. But while the personal pain of Ms. Schmidt's characters is palpable, it is never burdensome. Using language that is precise and descriptive, she maintains a sense of the absurd throughout. However, what is perhaps most striking is the uncompromisingly honest yet forgiving nature of Ms. Schmidt's approach. Although Kate wishes she could stay at a distance from the histrionics of her parents, she finally accepts, and is even comforted by, the knowledge that one never outgrows one's family. "For a moment I had stepped inside their circle and felt its narcotic comfort," says Kate in the final story, in which her grandmother faces death. "I was glad, suddenly, to be home, to be sharing the glory of disaster." "The Rose Thieves" is a graceful journey into the individual life of a young woman and the collective life of a family -- and a fine debut.

author: Beverly Fields
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE TALES OF ARTURO VIVANTE.  Edited by Mary Kinzie. (Sheep Meadow Press, Cloth, $24.95; Paper, $15.95.) These 35 short narratives by Arturo Vivante are aptly presented as tales, experiences told, with the double force of memory and invention. The variously named protagonists, like the first-person narrators, appear to be avatars of the author, remembering and touching up significant places in his life. Most frequently these are the landscapes of Italy, chiefly the Siena countryside, the scene of Mr. Vivante's childhood and early youth. The book's most vivid figure is the philosopher-father, perceived in the story called "The Orchard" almost as a fertility god, an extravagant planter of fruit trees, sustained by peaches and perhaps even more by the sight of the young women who gather them. The other side of his nature -- the aloof, crotchety parent -- emerges in "The Soft Core," in which, nevertheless, the son finally moves him to an affectionate response. The wrench of these father-son encounters is not the only tender spot in the collection, which also pays tribute to the gallantry and creative spirit of Mr. Vivante's mother and sister. There is recurrent homage to the English poets as well, and to Keats in particular, shown most clearly in "The Nightingale," a small parable of the writer's longing to express the inexpressible. Although some of the selections in "The Tales of Arturo Vivante" draw upon the many years the author has spent in the United States as a writer and teacher, it is the older, Italian memories that hold the imagination. Versions of all but one of these narratives, a selection from more than 30 years' work, have been printed separately before. It is a pleasure to find them here together.

FLAWLESS JADE.  By Barbara Hanrahan. (University of Queensland Press/International Specialized Book Service, 5602 Hassolo Street N.E., Portland, Ore. 97213, Paper, $12.95.) In her latest novel, the Australian writer Barbara Hanrahan reveals her concerns with life's contradictions and the nature of memory, particularly memories of childhood. But while her previous books have featured women in Australian and English settings, in "Flawless Jade" she turns to the Far East of the 1940's and 50's, as seen through the eyes of a young Chinese girl, Wing-yee. Born during "the Japanese War," Wing-yee lives through Mao Zedong's overthrow of Chiang Kai-shek and the Communist occupation of Canton. After fleeing with some of her family to an ostensibly better life in Hong Kong, she works as a servant, an embroiderer and, at 13, an usherette at the Golden Dragon Cinema. As time passes, Wing-yee's fantasies of returning to Canton gradually dissolve. She also experiences her first love -- and her first heartbreak. When she is 15, her mother crushes her aspirations to become an actress (she has sent a photograph to a movie company, using the name Flawless Jade), insisting that "unless you sold your body you couldn't become famous." Wing-yee's story is a modest 

Bildungsroman

, a poetic account of political and personal tumult and the human will to survive, of its heroine's efforts to make "even my bitter memories . . . somehow sweet." Ms. Hanrahan's book credibly portrays the stratified, male-dominated culture in which Wing-yee lives, a society in which, as she explains without self-pity, "a boy was better than a girl. . . . Girls were regarded as really quite useless." Its plain, straightforward style affectingly conveys the menace and futility of her world. At the book's conclusion, though years have passed, Wing-yee still waits hopefully for her "better future" to begin, studying English and dreaming of Hollywood. While this future appears doubtful, the story she tells assures that she will transcend it. For, as Ms. Hanrahan implies, by expressing ourselves we can triumph over the constraints of both culture and history.

pull_quote: LOOSE BALLS: The Short, Wild Life of the American Basketball Association.  By Terry Pluto. (Simon & Schuster, $22.95.) Surely the American Basketball Association deserves better. This was a league, after all, that gave the professional game Julius Erving, Moses Malone and Connie Hawkins; the three-point shot; faster, wide-open above-the-rim action; the slam-dunk contest, and the All-Star weekend. Although the league's coverage from its inception on a Friday the 13th in 1967 to its demise in 1976 was minuscule, tales of prowess on the court and mishaps off (and on) it have become legendary. Like Julius Erving's revolutionary dunks and the Indiana Pacers' Boston Celtics-like championship esprit de corps. Or the San Diego Conquistadors' coach, Wilt Chamberlain, who described one of his players as a "fat pig" and once showed up for a game at halftime. Or the night a New York Nets player sat on the bench in Long Island's frigid Commack Arena wearing an overcoat. (He refused to take it off until the team owner ordered him into the game.) In another game, the ace jump shooter and notorious flake Johnny Neumann was summoned from the bench and pulled off his sweat pants, only to reveal he was wearing nothing but a jockstrap. Great stuff for a book, right? Except that Terry Pluto throws up a brick by not even bothering to write a book. Instead, Mr. Pluto, a sportswriter for The Akron (Ohio) Beacon-Journal, has collected interviews with dozens of A.B.A. survivors (though he did not talk to several key figures who are talked about by the others), chopped them into paragraphs and strung them out in "Loose Balls." If Mr. Pluto's literary effort had an equivalent on the basketball court, he wouldn't have even made the Anaheim Amigos. Or the Minnesota Muskies.

Ronald Jager, a former professor of philosophy at Yale University, grew up in a farming community that felt it stood square with the world. Eighty acres is a small farm. The universe Mr. Jager's memoir discovers in this tiny parcel of land is multifarious and immense. "Eighty Acres" is rich with descriptive details. It tells us what it is like to follow a horse-drawn plow turning the earth, what it is to harvest wild berries, pitch freshly mown hay into the wagon, hunt hares in the fields, dry apples over the stove -- all of the day-to-day charms as well as the heavy labors of what is now an incredibly remote way of life. Set largely in the 1930's and 40's in lower Michigan, the life Mr. Jager describes so vividly might have continued but for the shocks of Depression and war. The three proverbial challenges of farming -- cash flow, overhead and capital investment -- so finely balanced on the diversified small farm of that era, were rendered all but insurmountable by the postwar economies of scale enforced on even its smallest cultivations. "Eighty Acres" is nostalgic in the best sense, elegiac in the way it honors the author's close-knit family, tied in its every aspect to the earth. A moving evocation of its time and place, this book is also a valuable description of the fundamentals of sensible, sustainable agriculture once widely practiced on American farms. Mr. Jager's memoir is full of life, an act of preservation tendered to us from an irresistible perspective of love.

Wayne Johnson's first novel illuminates the lives of a group of Ojibwa and Chippewa Indians in the lake country of northern Minnesota from the 1950's to the 1980's, revealing a world of guns and taverns and too much liquor, of grown men's anger turned on sons, wives and friends. Each of the 19 chapters takes place in a different year, and each focuses on different incidents in the lives of the novel's characters. Mr. Johnson uses both first- and third-person voices to tell their many stories. Among the most successful are his account of young Red Deer, who uses his skills as a baseball pitcher to vent his rage, and of Eli, whose pride in his welding skill enables him to transcend personal tragedies. But don't expect to find any levity in "The Snake Game," or to meet any women of substance. Dominated -- sometimes beaten -- by their men, the women wait meekly for drunken lovers, conjure spells to seduce objects of sexual desire or arrive in boatloads to service carousing fishermen from the city. Because Mr. Johnson writes so well, I wish he'd had a crankier editor -- to take care of puzzling lines like "The horn jabbed him like electricity" and to question bits of unfinished plot. Any author would be challenged by the prospect of inhabiting the lives of so many characters, and sometimes Mr. Johnson fails to bring all of them equally to life. He is most at ease when writing about a young outsider named Marty Sorenson, who seems to be something of an alter ego. Yet even when Marty and the others falter as characters, it is clear that Mr. Johnson cares for them and feels deeply the pain of their lives.

author: Alison Knopf
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: STANLEY: The Making of an African Explorer.  By Frank McLynn. (Scarborough House, $23.95.) Henry M. Stanley, best remembered for saying "Dr. Livingstone, I presume?," was such an eccentric character -- brave, paranoid, oversensitive and articulate -- that he is worth knowing better. The biographer Frank McLynn, in his highly readable "Stanley: The Making of an African Explorer," presents a driven, determined man who was secretly tortured by insecurities, guilt and conflicting desires. A latent homosexual given to beating his delicate acolytes, Stanley was terrified of women, regarding them either as high-born ladies to be worshiped or as whores. Stanley always seemed to prefer adventure in the company of men to pursuing his ill-fated relationships with women. His childhood may explain his later problems: he was illegitimate (he changed his name from John Rowlands as a teen-ager) and passed from relative to relative until, as a 7-year old, he was consigned to a workhouse in Wales. But in his brief friendship with David Livingstone, who had rejected Europeand society -- and women -- to find the source of the Nile, Stanley found a kindred spirit. It is typical of Stanley's convoluted hypocrisy that he could not confess to his friend the real reason for having tracked him down in Africa: The New York Herald paid for Stanley's entire expedition in exchange for the exclusive story. Instead, he told Livingstone that the newspaper had paid for the trip as a charitable act, in order to get supplies to the stranded missionary. He set off for Africa a second time, after Livingstone's death; this trip took him across the entire African continent. Only by submerging himself in a life of constant danger was he able to escape his inner turmoil. But with this psychic relief came cruelty. Many men died on behalf of Stanley's determination to keep moving; some he simply abandoned when they were too sick to move. Stanley was a remarkably bold liar and bluffer; he even lied in his own diary. Mr. McLynn, however, has taken care not to fall into any traps, and the entertaining text is well documented with footnotes.
headline: IN SHORT: NONFICTION

title: Opening Night On Broadway
author: Steven Suskin

There are few who would deny that Broadway's greatest gift to the world has been the musical comedy, and perhaps fewer still who would dispute that this decidedly American concoction reached its peak in the middle of this century. Among its many other virtues as a comprehensive research tool, or just as a delight for theater aficionados, "Opening Night on Broadway" by Steven Suskin, a theatrical producer and manager, confirms that the critics were definitely aware something special was happening on the Great White Way at the time. As Brooks Atkinson wrote about "Finian's Rainbow," which opened in 1947, four years after the pivotal "Oklahoma!": "If the American musical stage continues to improve, it will no longer be necessary for anyone to speak dialogue on the stage. Everything essential can be said in song and dancing." From "Alive and Kicking" to "Ziegfeld Follies of 1957," this collection of excerpts from the daily reviews constitutes a galvanizing parade of the peacocks as well as the turkeys. Though the era encompassed practically every great musical our generation knows by name (including "Guys and Dolls," "How to Succeed in Business Without Really Trying," "The Music Man," "My Fair Lady," "The Pajama Game," "West Side Story" and "Hello, Dolly!"), typically it was the less successful shows that inspired the wittiest comments. Consider the cavalcade of puns on titles, including Walter Kerr's "Anyone can whistle, but nobody can sing"; Robert Coleman's "Lerner, Loewe, and Hart spent so much to mount    Camelot    that the wisecrackers have been calling it 'Costallot' "; Howard Barnes's response to "Let's Make an Opera": "Let's not!"; and Louis Kronenberger's revised name for "The Girl From Nantucket": "The Girl From Death Valley." In response to this last woebegone offering, Wilella Waldorf of The New York Post was even more vicious: "If the producers wish to lift something from this review for advertising purposes, they may quote us as saying, 'It lacks everything.' "

title: Through And Through: Toledo Stories
author: Stan Friedman
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THROUGH AND THROUGH: Toledo Stories.  By Joseph Geha. (Graywolf, Paper, $7.95.) A new town is a blue town to begin with, but if that town is Toledo, Ohio, and you are a new arrival in the Glass Capital's Arab community, the transition can be especially melancholy. Such is Joseph Geha's message in his first book of short stories. Mr. Geha's characters are butchers and debkee dancers, mustachioed relatives (of both genders) and married strangers -- even a murderer who seeks redemption from an apparition of Christ that appears on a storage tank. With the exception of the title piece, in which that vision-seeking killer reflects upon a treacherous career, the stories have a similar structure, emerging as slice-of-life tales viewed from a street corner or through a window. Often, we come upon scenes we fear we've seen somewhere before, then are saved by the author's neat sense of detail. "Everything, Everything," for example, explores a young woman's loneliness through an encounter with a handsome stranger she meets in a laundromat. When one of her brassieres ends up in his basket, our attention is focused on her hand, which moves side to side as if "erasing a blackboard," trying to undo the mistake. In "Monkey Business," a widowed father hesitantly succumbs to Uhdrah, the woman brought by a matchmaker from the old country to be his second wife. Meanwhile his son, Jameel, spends his days mimicking the movements of Asfoori, a local derelict. An overt irony, the father bending to Uhdrah's wishes at the same time that Asfoori -- like Uhdrah a representative of Old World values -- falls over dead, is transformed into black comedy with Jameel's mindless aping of the derelict's death thrall as another bum, a war veteran, cries "Sniper!" and bystanders drop to the ground. When a foreign people inhabits a new place, both people and place risk losing their identity. Joseph Geha fights hard to keep his characters exotic, to make Toledo a land of mystery.
headline: IN SHORT: FICTION

title: Ludwig Wittgenstein: The Duty Of Genius
author: Ray Monk. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: LUDWIG WITTGENSTEIN  The Duty of Genius. By Ray Monk. Illustrated. 654 pp. New York: The Free Press. $29.95.    Ludwig Wittgenstein was the greatest philosopher of the 20th century. Many books have been written about his philosophy. Ray Monk's "Ludwig Wittgenstein" is the first substantial biography of his whole life. It is not a book to which one would turn to learn about Wittgenstein's thought, but enough is said about the philosophical writings to make intelligible the story of the philosopher's life. And the story is well told; the narrative is vivid, clear, sympathetic and credible.   Wittgenstein's great-grandfather was a land agent named Moses Maier, who in 1808 took the name of his princely employers, the Wittgensteins. His father, Karl, a friend of Johannes Brahms, was the most acute industrialist in the Austrian steel industry; he made the family the Austrian equivalent of the Carnegies or Rothschilds. He had five sons and three daughters by a Roman Catholic wife, and baptized all of them into the Catholic faith. He set out to educate the sons in a very severe regime which would turn them into captains of industry. He did not succeed. Three of the sons committed suicide; the fourth, Paul, became (despite the loss of an arm in World War I) a concert pianist; the fifth, the youngest child, born in Vienna in 1889, was the philosopher.   Ludwig Wittgenstein attended the Realschule in Linz, where he was a contemporary of Adolf Hitler. He was a poor scholar, teased by his peers. At school he also lost his faith. The major intellectual influences on him in his youth, apart from the philosophical works of Schopenhauer, were the physicist Ludwig Boltzmann (suicide 1906) and the psychologist Otto Weininger (suicide 1903).   Mr. Monk believes that Weininger's bizarre book "Sex and Character" was of fundamental importance in shaping Wittgenstein's career. According to Weininger -- a homosexual -- all human beings are bisexual, a mixture of male and female. Woman is nothing but sexuality: every woman is a mixture of prostitute and mother. Men must choose between the masculine and feminine elements within themselves; the ideal for a man is to free himself from sex. "The choice that Weininger's theory offers is a bleak and terrible one indeed: genius or death," says Mr. Monk. "If . . . one cannot free oneself from sensuality and earthly desires -- then one has no right to live at all."   For Wittgenstein, to acquire genius became a categorical imperative. He once described Beethoven greeting a friend on completion of a new fugue: he "came to the door, looking as if he had been fighting the devil, and having eaten nothing for 36 hours because his cook and parlour-maid had been away from his rage. That's the sort of man to be."   It was in Cambridge in 1911 that Wittgenstein first gave evidence of genius in philosophy, and it was Bertrand Russell who first recognized it. Wittgenstein was, Russell wrote, "perhaps the most perfect example I have ever known of genius as traditionally conceived, passionate, profound, intense, and dominating." Russell was already well known as the author of powerful, original work in logic and mathematics; he soon realized that Wittgenstein's gifts were greater than his own, and he devoted himself with great generosity to their development. In 1912 he told Wittgenstein's sister, "We expect the next big step in philosophy to be taken by your brother."   The expectation was fulfilled, but Wittgenstein's philosophical message was not given to the world until after World War I. During that war he served in the Austrian Army on the Eastern and Italian fronts, and much of the material that later appeared in his masterpiece, "Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus," was written while on active service. At the front Wittgenstein showed conspicuous courage and was commended and decorated; he was also converted, by the reading of Tolstoy, to an intense though idiosyncratic Christianity. "Perhaps the nearness of death," he wrote in his diary, "will bring me the light of life. May God enlighten me. I am a worm, but through God I become a man. God be with me. Amen."   After the war, having inherited a share of his father's fortune, he found himself one of the wealthiest men in Europe. Within a month of returning from the army he gave all his money away. For some years he supported himself as a gardener or as a schoolmaster in rural Austrian schools. He believed, for a while, that he had already solved all the problems of philosophy in his "Tractatus," which appeared (after great difficulty in finding a publisher) in German in 1921 and in English in 1922. The book quickly became famous; though it was itself metaphysical and almost mystical, as well as austerely logical, it was most admired by the anti-metaphysical positivists of the Vienna Circle.    It was at Vienna that Wittgenstein returned to the study of philosophy, when his career as a schoolmaster came to an unhappy end after allegations of cruelty to his pupils. Eventually he returned to Cambridge and during his years there in the 1930's he became the most influential teacher of philosophy in Britain. The philosophy he taught in this period differed from that published in the "Tractatus"; it was not presented in print until "Philosophical Investigations" was published posthumously in 1953.   After the Anschluss, Hitler's forced unification of Austria and Germany in 1938, Wittgenstein became a British citizen. During World War II he worked as a paramedic, and in 1947 he resigned his Cambridge chair. He continued to write philosophy and to communicate philosophical thoughts to close friends and disciples. After a period of solitary life in Ireland, he stayed in the houses of various friends in Oxford and Cambridge until his death in 1951 at the age of 62. He left a mass of philosophical papers, many of them still awaiting publication.   Wittgenstein's genius is patent to any philosopher who will take the time and trouble to come to grips with his profound but difficult writings. His life, as described by Mr. Monk, seems to have been a lonely and tragic one. He was often tormented by temptations to suicide, and was sometimes on the verge of mental illness. He regarded his life as a professor as "a living death," and held many of his colleagues, in the various callings he pursued, in loathing and contempt. His only philosophical peer was Russell, and the relationship between the two soured after Wittgenstein's return to Cambridge. Many of his philosophical disciples loved him, but it was a love mixed strongly with fear.   Four times in his life, according to Mr. Monk, Wittgenstein fell deeply in love. Three of his loves were male and one female. (Sensational stories have been told of Wittgenstein's passion for rough homosexuals picked up in Vienna parks; Mr. Monk examines the evidence patiently and convincingly and concludes that any such encounters took place only in Wittgenstein's own fantasy.) David Pinsent, to whose memory the "Tractatus" was dedicated, accompanied Wittgenstein to Norway and Iceland in the prewar period; he was killed in 1918. Francis Skinner, who came up to Cambridge as a student in 1930, had an all-absorbing relationship with Wittgenstein in the 30's; and in 1946 Wittgenstein fell in love with a Cambridge medical student, Ben Richards, 40 years his junior.   MANY readers will be surprised to learn from Mr. Monk's book that there was a time when Wittgenstein had plans to marry. From 1926 to 1931 he had a friendship with a Swiss woman, Marguerite Respinger. For a period he wrote to her almost daily, and he sculpted a bust of her. An entry in his diary for 1930 reads: "Arrived back in Cambridge after the Easter vacation. In Vienna often with Marguerite. Easter Sunday with her in Neuwaldegg. For three hours we kissed each other a great deal and it was very nice."   Once it became clear that Wittgenstein wanted to marry her, Marguerite drew back -- especially as it transpired that what the philosopher had in mind was a Platonic, childless union.   Faith in God was important to Wittgenstein; but his faith seems to have been a somber one. God was perhaps no more than Fate. If He was to be thought of as a person, it was solely as a severe judge. Yet Wittgenstein's last words were, "Tell  [ my friends ]  I've had a wonderful life." Ray Monk's book has succeeded remarkably in portraying some of its wonders.    HE WELCOMED THE BOMB    Wittgenstein's hostility towards professional philosophy and his dislike of Cambridge remained constant throughout his academic career, but in the years . . . that followed the Second World War, they seemed to become fused with a kind of apocalyptic vision. . . .   What links this apocalyptic anxiety with his hostility to academic philosophy is his detestation of the power of science in our age, which on the one hand encouraged the philosopher's "craving for generality," and on the other produced the atomic bomb. . . . He even welcomed the bomb, if only the fear of it could do something to diminish the reverence with which society regarded scientific progress. . . . The most pessimistic view, for him, was one which foresaw the triumph of science and technology: "Science and industry, and their progress, might turn out to be the most enduring thing in the modern world. Perhaps any speculation about a coming collapse of science and industry is . . . nothing but a dream; perhaps science and industry, having caused infinite misery in the process, will unite the world -- I mean condense it into a single unit, though one in which peace is the last thing that will find a home. Because science and industry do decide wars, or so it seems."     From "Ludwig Wittgenstein."

pull_quote: PIZZA IN PUSHKIN SQUARE: What Russians Think About Americans and the American Way of Life.  By Victor Ripp. (Simon & Schuster, $18.95.) Victor Ripp, an American academic of Russian descent, employs the travelogue genre to track down the misconceptions that, glasnost notwithstanding, continue to cloud the Soviet view of America. In his travels, Mr. Ripp meets a schoolboy who asks about the cowboys and Indians in today's Texas. He meets a Moscow woman who at first seems well informed about America, but then assumes that Mr. Ripp's home in Hopewell, N.J., is a summer    dacha.    And he finds himself in a great number of awkward situations caused by cultural misunderstandings between him and his Russian friends. All of this is amusing, albeit for the most part predictable. Unfortunately, the two elements in Mr. Ripp's scheme -- the misconceptions and the historical roots of these misconceptions -- do not fall together into a uniform narrative, and the sarcastic tone of "Pizza in Pushkin Square," while initially amusing, quickly becomes an annoyance. The author's tendency to jump to unjustified, sweeping conclusions is even more irritating. A decade or two ago, casual observers seemed to have little trouble noting undiscovered traits of Russian character and style. Today, with everybody Moscow-bound, even informed travelers like Mr. Ripp seem to be hard pressed to bring back anything of value.

title: Hollywood Gothic
author: David J Skal
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: Undying fans of "Dracula" will relish this account of how the hairy-palmed, stench-ridden, cadaverous shade who flowed in 1897 from Bram Stoker's pen became an elegantly dressed stiff who slips into dark bedrooms by the flickering light of television sets. In HOLLYWOOD GOTHIC: The Tangled Web of "Dracula" From Novel to Stage to Screen (Norton, $39.95), the novelist David J. Skal tracks Transylvania's most popular vampire with dry wit and the skills of a fine detective. He follows the efforts of Stoker's widow, Florence, to consign to flames every existing print of "Nosferatu," F. W. Murnau's unauthorized 1922 silent film version of the story (at least one of which, mercifully, escaped her clutches). He stalks "Dracula" from London to the Broadway stage, where the bloodthirsty Count claimed the body of a Hungarian actor named Bela Lugosi, making him forever captive to the role. Mr. Skal reveals the heretofore hidden intrigues that landed Stoker's novel in Hollywood, where Lugosi's heirs would eventually lose their 16-year struggle with Universal Pictures to possess their father's image beyond the grave. But the author is most satisfying when he reveals his discovery, in a Cuban film vault, of the missing reel of a Spanish-language "Dracula" that was filmed in tandem with Tod Browning's 1931 American release. Filled with charming and unusual illustrations, the volume includes a handy chronology ("Dracula at a Glance") and many incisive observations about the terror and appeal of mixing sex with immortality. Yet Mr. Skal wisely treads lightly over the meaning of "Dracula," leaving its essential mystery undisturbed. Indeed, those who cannot find their own reflection in Bram Stoker's still-living creation are surely the undead.

Availing himself of his rich family history, Terry Kay uses his fourth novel to tell an admittedly autobiographical story in which he celebrates his parents' marriage. "There was a grand romance of life between them," Mr. Kay states in an author's note at the end of the book, "and my father's loneliness following the death of my mother was a terrible experience for him." The novel explores how 81-year-old Sam Peek, hobbled by a bad leg and dependent on a walker, manages to carry on after the death of Cora, his wife of 57 years. Feisty and determined, Sam continues to drive his rattletrap truck to his pecan grove to tend the trees. He makes plans to travel to a nearby town in Georgia for his 60th college reunion. He keeps a journal. And he tries to outwit his two daughters, worrywarts whose mollycoddling grows irritating even to the reader. What ultimately saves Sam, though, is a magnificent and mysterious white dog -- perhaps the manifestation of Cora's gallant spirit -- whose companionship eases his loneliness and thus encourages him to maintain his independence. Despite a few monotonous characterizations and some banal journal entries, "To Dance With the White Dog" is a deftly shaped and vivid book. In this memorable novel, Terry Kay has created a tender and bracing tale of an octogenarian fighting to live a connected and purposeful life.

One of the first surprises law students encounter in their course on constitutional law is that the First Amendment, as interpreted over the years by even the most liberal judges, doesn't give someone an absolute right to speak or write freely. Long before entering law school, most students have heard that free expression doesn't allow a person to shout "Fire!" in a crowded theater falsely. In addition to reasons of public safety, other limitations have been imposed by statutes and the courts, including laws against libel, invasion of privacy, blackmail and fraud.    A few more surprises are in store for readers of Steven H. Shiffrin's "First Amendment, Democracy and Romance." The biggest one is that his First Amendment exemplars aren't such history-making United States Supreme Court justices as Oliver Wendell Holmes and William J. Brennan but Walt Whitman and Ralph Waldo Emerson.

pull_quote: BRADOVICH.  By William Herrick. (New Directions, $18.95.) In many ways, William Herrick's 10th novel conforms to the Pop Fiction Code. Stephen Bradovich, a craggy, widowed football player turned sculptor, lives in a city that purports to be New York but feels, with its cozy neighborliness and broad boulevards, like a dream. Here the hero is pursued by a supernaturally effective enemy called "The Authority." But instead of being the homage to Franz Kafka that the author clearly intended, the novel equally suggests Judith Krantz, featuring the sort of writing in which meals are described to the last crumb, yet logic evaporates at will. (Thwarted when he tries to book his escape at a travel agency or by phone, our hero never thinks simply to get in a bus, train or taxi, to rent a car or take himself directly to an airport.) Although it's a suspense novel, "Bradovich" is not intended to be commercial fiction; its dropped names are not those of brands beloved by Best-Selling Authors but those adored in our universities. And Mr. Herrick's pages are peppered with philosophizing about Life's Meaning and paeans to Great Art. So the really scary thing about this book is not the depredations capriciously wreaked by "The Authority," not the whipping, incest, bestiality, rape, mutilation and kinky sex that keep popping up, not death and its injustice, but rather the fact that New Directions, a house renowned for publishing writers like Jorge Luis Borges, Delmore Schwartz, Kay Boyle, Tennessee Williams and Jean Cocteau, is now offering thinking readers novels as meretricious as this one.

pull_quote: WATER BABY: The Story of Alvin.  By Victoria A. Kaharl. (Oxford University, $21.95.) This is a fascinating history of Alvin, the world's first deep-diving submarine. The three-person craft, which opened the ocean depths to exploration in the mid-1960's, has shown scientists strange and previously unknown worlds and in the process helped alter our understanding of planet Earth. "Water Baby," by the science writer Victoria A. Kaharl, is, however, much more than a story about a titanium sphere with a curious name. It is also about the men and women who, during dives so deep it takes hours to surface, must trust that Alvin will protect them from thousands of pounds of pressure on each square inch of the hull. There is heroism as well as humor: stories of pilots jockeying the craft free from fissures more than 8,000 feet down, for example, and a running account of the motley crew of Alvin's mother ship, including a man nicknamed Bare Bear who slept in his bunk with a teddy bear. The best parts of "Water Baby" are the vivid descriptions of trips to the sea floor. Early in its career, Alvin had shown scientists that the deep ocean was not barren, as had been believed, but was teeming with life. However, even veterans of deep diving were surprised at the lushness of marine oases at the bottom of the Pacific, which they viewed in the mid-70's, courtesy of Alvin. "Water Baby" does bog down in places, but the information overkill is clearly the result of the author's extensive research and love for the subject. In the end, Ms. Kaharl's enthusiasm proves to be irresistible.

author: Nina Sonenberg

pull_quote: LANDSCAPE: MEMORY.  By Matthew Stadler. (Scribner's, $19.95.) The year is 1915. Nine years after the great earthquake, San Francisco is hosting a world's fair, Model T's and trench warfare have captured the popular imagination and the hero of Matthew Stadler's first novel is coming of age. "Landscape: Memory" is a portrait of the artist as a painfully sensitive young man, a richly impressionistic tale told in the form of a private journal and illustrated with Mr. Stadler's renditions of the narrator's painting-in-progress. Young Maxwell Kosegarten is a survivor of the great 1906 earthquake. He and his best friend, Duncan, brought together by the disaster, now spend their days exploring a changed San Francisco. They trace the quake's path along the coast, wander through the glittering fair at night and puzzle over their own shared recollections of the past. The process of memory is Max's true fascination: he struggles to fix dynamic events and impressions in his journal just as he yearns to capture a changing landscape in paint. The book remains a bit sketchy and disorienting until Max succeeds in bringing the reader closer to his private world. But the outside world is always interesting, as Mr. Stadler subtly weaves accurate historical details into Max's accounts of his daily experiences. This vivid narrative scene-painting brings a lost era to life, encompassing the thrill of a first automobile ride, the increasing horror of news from the European front and a child's terror as the earth rips apart. Max's memory of the earthquake unfolds late in the book, but it finally allows us to enter his emotional landscape, even as human figures begin to appear in his painting. When Duncan comes closer too, becoming lover as well as friend, the stage is set for passion and tragedy. "Landscape: Memory" is an unusual and impressive debut, a book that takes both a young man and his city through pain toward maturity.

title: Bloomsbury Reflections
author: Alen Macweeney
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: Vanessa Bell once said that the subject matter of photography should be a little absurd. By this, Bell may have been thinking of her great-aunt, the Victorian photographer Julia Margaret Cameron, "who posed her sitters in a 'high-art' mode, and whose aim was not merely to 'take' photographs but to immortalize those dragooned into posing for her," writes Frances Spalding in her brief, discerning foreword to BLOOMSBURY REFLECTIONS (Norton, $39.95), a collection of photographs of the friends and descendants of the Bloomsbury group. Likewise, Bell would have appreciated the photographer Alen MacWeeney's slightly absurd -- though exceptionally beautiful -- photographic portraits. Each, despite its appearance of spontaneity, has been composed with great artifice. Each of his pictures is a collage of allusions, a reference to the past, while at the same time a frozen moment revealing something essential about the sitter's character. To this end he makes use not just of color and light, but of the furniture, decorative objects and paintings of Bloomsbury. Among the book's most memorable photos, in fact, are his eerily evocative shots of such Bloomsbury haunts as Monk's House, where Virginia Woolf did much of her writing, and Charleston, the country home of Clive and Vanessa Bell. Unfortunately, while the photographs draw us in, the text, which largely consists of a brief reminiscence of Bloomsbury by each sitter, is far less absorbing. Even readers who normally subscribe to the cult of Bloomsbury will question the value of such banal revelations as that of Cecil Woolf, who recalls seeing his Uncle Leonard pick up a piece of chocolate from the floor of a theater and "pop it in his mouth," or Henrietta Garnett, who remembers that her grandmother Vanessa Bell was so frugal that she served "dessert at lunch, but none at dinner." The problem with most of these pieces, written by Sue Allison, a reporter at Life magazine, is that the speakers are of a different generation from the principals of Bloomsbury. With the exception of Quentin Bell, who speaks engagingly of life at Charleston, their memories are at best fragmentary, at worst too subjective to be revealing. Fortunately, Mr. MacWeeney's strangely canny photographs work independently of the text. While "Bloomsbury Reflections" reveals little of the actual stories behind these often guarded faces, it is a stunning visual record of what was once the spirit of Bloomsbury.
headline: Woolfs Under Glass

title: Angels: An Endangered Species
author: Malcolm Godwin
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: ANGELS: An Endangered Species.  By Malcolm Godwin. (Simon & Schuster, $19.95.) Angels are all around us -- in movies ("Angels With Dirty Faces"), sports (California Angels), even law enforcement (Guardian Angels). Angels figure in our most rarefied worship and in everyday figures of speech. They appear in many guises, from ancient bringers of glad tidings to modern comic-book heroes who appear in the nick of time to rescue good and defeat evil. Artists have been known to spend lifetimes creating substantial representations of these insubstantial beings. But are angels merely figments of our collective imaginations, inspired by legend and fostered by religion? That is a question not easily answered without serious study of the delightful "Angels: An Endangered Species." Malcolm Godwin begins by discussing such cloud-shaking matters as just how seraphim are distinct from cherubim, who are in turn quite separate from archangels. Understanding this heavenly hierarchy creates an important foundation for our knowledge of the more advanced material concerning these winged messengers. But winged messengers from whom, what or where? The author, a British artist and lecturer, presents cases in which encounter and speculation in some way transform those who have been witness to angelic presences. If angels are real, could they appear in other forms -- as unidentified flying objects, for instance? And if real, how do they fly? Are those dainty, feathered shoulder appendages aerodynamically adequate? Just what did Ezekiel see in that fiery chariot, up in the air? Could the legends of the lost continent of Mu be based on fact? Obviously, the questions surrounding these issues require further study by angelic scholars. Tongue parked firmly in cheek, Mr. Godwin takes us through the intricacies of modern angelology and a good deal of our own history, using text, charts, drawings and glorious illustrations. As to whether angels are real or not, endangered or not, Mr. Godwin leaves that up to his readers to discover in this heavenly book.

title: Before The Storm
author: Marion Donhoff
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: BEFORE THE STORM: Memories of My Youth in Old Prussia.  By Marion, Countess Donhoff. Translated by Jean Steinberg. (Knopf, $22.95.) The way Marion Donhoff grew up is probably as foreign to most Americans as life in a novel by Goethe; it was certainly as romantic. The Countess, who is now the publisher of the Hamburg weekly Die Zeit, was the youngest daughter of an East Prussian family whose genealogical tree branched back to the Knights of the Teutonic Order, and she had the run of a castle and grounds visitors called "more beautiful than Versailles." Indeed, with the disappearance of East Prussia -- at the end of World War II, its castles were leveled and its land ceded to Poland -- the kind of childhood Countess Donhoff had has become something foreign to everyone. Whence the interest of "Before the Storm": it documents in knowing detail a semifeudal world most of us have glimpsed only in movies and caricatures, a world of kindly, paternalistic aristocrats and their class-conscious servants. "The cook would never have sat down to eat with the kitchen maids, nor the housekeeper with the housemaids," she writes; "the cook and the housekeeper ate in a separate room at a table to which only my mother's maid . . .  [ was ]  admitted." The tone of these memoirs, ably translated by Jean Steinberg, is unabashedly nostalgic, even, at times, defensive; the Countess's parents entertained lavishly, she tells us, but they lived austerely, and the children always rode third class. Countess Donhoff, however, is not sentimental. She frankly acknowledges the anti-Semitism of her parents' class, although, she explains, they also hated the Nazis. But the most powerful part of this book narrates her 1945 flight westward before the Red Army and the utter collapse of all she knew. "The end of East Prussia," she writes, "had come down to this: three dying soldiers trying to drag themselves across the Nogat bridge . . . and a woman on horseback, whose ancestors had come from the west into the wilderness east of this river six hundred years ago, riding back to the west -- six hundred years of history wiped out."

pull_quote: PORTABLE PEOPLE.  By Paul West. (Paris Review, Paper, $10.95.) All of us create for ourselves private pantheons inhabited by people we have never met but who nevertheless have left indelible impressions. Many of them live as vividly for us as people we encounter in daily life. The novelist Paul West shares with us his personal register of celebrities in "Portable People," a sly and witty updating of Aubrey's "Brief Lives." His 82 subjects range from Keats to Marlene Dietrich, Rodin to Chris Evert, Count Basie to Nabokov. His selections include artists, scientists, writers, musicians, athletes, statesmen, actors and a generous sprinkling of aviators. The archest of the lot present the subject speaking to us in the first person (Colette reflecting orgiastically on food, for one, or Richard Nixon on his Chinese hosts). The strongest contain memorable epigrams. Here, for example, is West on Evonne Goolagong: "Listen to her name: a puddle with a chime in it." And on Chris Evert: "Taut and tight-lipped mistress of the baseline, she is the all-American golden girl become the champion of monotony." Mr. West is most incisive about subjects that he takes most seriously: Simone Weil or Maurice Maeterlinck, Edith Sitwell or Samuel Beckett -- who, says Mr. West, "became a Frenchman so as to have no home to go to." Joe Servello's illustrations are sometimes inspired.

A common criticism of today's musical theater is that emphasis is placed on spectacle above all else. One acid crack hurled now is that the audience leaves the theater humming the scenery. But in post-World War II America, when theatergoers left a Lerner and Loewe musical there was no question what was on their minds and lips: the fairy-tale stories and witty lyrics of Alan Jay Lerner and the beautiful music of Fritz Loewe. In "Inventing Champagne," Gene Lees reminds us of the phenomenal impact of the creators of the musicals "Brigadoon," "My Fair Lady" and "Camelot." Mr. Lees, the author of "Oscar Peterson" and "Singers and the Song," is in his element writing of the horrific rehearsals and openings of "My Fair Lady" and "Camelot." Prior to its New York opening, "Camelot" played in Toronto. Not only did the show run four and a half hours there, but Lerner entered the hospital with a bleeding ulcer, soon to be followed by the show's director, Moss Hart, who suffered his second coronary thrombosis. Despite Lerner and Loewe's professional and personal problems (Lerner was married eight times and was addicted to drugs), their musicals were what America saw, listened to and talked about. They, along with a handful of other librettists, lyricists and composers, helped define American popular culture.

title: The Power And The Glitter
author: Ronald Brownstein. Illustrated.
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: THE POWER AND THE GLITTER The Hollywood-Washington Connection. By Ronald Brownstein. Illustrated. 437 pp. New York: Pantheon Books. $24.95.     In the early part of our century, before airplanes, interstate highways and the fund-raising brunch, the District of Columbia and Hollywood were two small towns with one thing in common: both spent much time and energy trying to divine the mood of the country. Beyond that, they had little active interest in each other. But by 1981 a movie star was in the White House, and by 1988 another movie star, Warren Beatty, was part of the inner circle of Gary Hart's Presidential campaign, developing strategy. Just how American politics has become so enmeshed with Hollywood is the subject of "The Power and the Glitter," Ronald Brownstein's fascinating account of what he terms in his subtitle "The Hollywood-Washington Connection."   As Mr. Brownstein shows, most of the Hollywood people involved in politics -- like the actress Helen Gahagan Douglas, who served in Congress in the 1940's, or Orson Welles, who toyed with the idea of running for Vice President in 1948 -- have been liberals. Yet the two who have got the farthest were not. George Murphy, the tap-dancer who made it to the Senate in the 1960's, and of course Ronald Reagan, who did even better, were men of the right. It is as if the public were saying to Hollywood: we'll take actors, but not the ones you want to offer us.   Currently, Hollywood's participation in national politics is centered on fund raising. Ideas certainly play a part (as they did during the Depression and World War II, when Hollywood's involvement was more ideological), but few candidates come to Southern California for counsel. They come for money -- and they get it, in large amounts. Hollywood's money-givers are not as bad as they might be, nor are they as vapid as Mr. Brownstein sometimes paints them. They are certainly not as venal as the gents who occupied the smoke-filled rooms of the past.    Apart from money, Hollywood can always provide glamour. "Hollywood's greatest creation is itself," Mr. Brownstein writes. And what are most American politicians but self-invented? Gary Hart sums up the political value of Hollywood celebrities to candidates this way: "It's a little bit like  [ the stars ]  are . . . saying, 'You know who I am, and I want to tell you about my friend. . . . I want you to support him.' It's almost a transfer."   Mr. Brownstein, a political correspondent for The Los Angeles Times, is an able guide through all of these thickets, and if he has his prejudices -- he's a liberal and, in the current fashion, is slightly contemptuous of modern Hollywood -- he has written a needed book, the first full-scale attempt that I know of to bring together this part of our modern history. The result is graceful and nuanced.   The history of the Hollywood-Washington connection, as Mr. Brownstein describes it, begins with Louis B. Mayer, the head of M-G-M, the mightiest of the studios, and Herbert Hoover. Mayer seemed to think that proximity to Hoover might help him associate with classier people than his everyday business provided, and he flattered and cajoled his way into the future President's favor. But if the connection started gently, even sleepily, it soon moved to activism, forced by the events of the 1930's and 1940's.    Hollywood lurched into electoral politics in the 1934 California gubernatorial race. The author Upton Sinclair ran on a populist platform that proposed increasing the taxes on the film studios. The response was "mogul politics . . . hard, shrewd, autocratic, and above all, coercive," culminating in a fabricated newsreel that was to prove significant in defeating Sinclair. The newsreel depicted wild-eyed, foreign-looking radicals happily anticipating Sinclair's socialist paradise. (Some of the footage was apparently lifted from a Warner Brothers feature film.) The result, for the studio chiefs, was a "political baptism," an involvement in politics that has only grown, never diminished.   During the war, those in the movie business, like most Americans, made common cause with the Government. But after the anti-Communist hearings of the House Committee on Un-American Activities got under way in the late 1940's and the subpoenas started arriving, many in Hollywood came to view the Government not as a partner or a benevolent father but as a danger. Prominent individuals in the movie community suffered under HUAC's thumb, while others cooperated with the committee or applauded it, and the divisions are still evident today.    Although there was very little effective fighting back, Mr. Brownstein describes how a Committee for the First Amendment was formed by John Huston, William Wyler and Philip Dunne. This group, with a brigade of movie stars, went to Washington in an ill-fated attempt to defend the so-called Hollywood Ten, the writers and directors who would soon be in prison for refusing to name names or say whether they had belonged to the Communist Party. If there is often an adversarial quality to Hollywood's dealings with Washington today, surely it began with the HUAC hearings.   During the early 40's, Hollywood was able to raise large sums of money very fast for the war effort. But it wasn't until the rise of television that modern Hollywood fund raising began to come into its own. The first political winner of the television age was John F. Kennedy, who, according to Mr. Brownstein and just about anyone who met Kennedy, treated Hollywood like a cross between a "fraternity and a brothel."    Mr. Brownstein hangs his narrative thread on personal alliances: Adlai Stevenson and Lauren Bacall, for example, or Warren Beatty and Gary Hart. In the case of Kennedy, he focuses on the President's relationship with Frank Sinatra, a relationship that he considers pivotal in the history of Hollywood and Washington. Mr. Sinatra and his rat pack of chums "embodied Hollywood's most elemental myth, its deepest unspoken appeal . . . a life without rules, without the constraints of fidelity, monogamy, sobriety." This was, as we now all know, dangerously close to Kennedy's own personal ethos. The Sinatra-Kennedy match was perfect for a while, each man drawing what he needed from the other. It was Mr. Sinatra who introduced Kennedy to Judith Exner, the young woman he had also introduced to the head of the Chicago mob. For a while she traveled between her two men. (If that's not a movie plot, I'll turn in my Guild card.)   At a higher level during this era, Arthur Krim, then head of United Artists, now of Orion Pictures, raised money for Kennedy and later became close to Lyndon Johnson. It was Mr. Krim, Mr. Brownstein relates in a particularly vivid section of his book, who brought Lew Wasserman, the legendary chief of MCA Inc. who is generally thought of as the last of the moguls, into active participation in the Democratic party, ushering in the era of serious Hollywood fund raising.   Mr. Brownstein is a little hard on some of the players in his tale -- Norman Lear, for one, may have reason to complain about unnecessary roughness -- but there is no denying that fund raising in Los Angeles has its bizarre features. Any candidate, for almost any race, with the slightest claim on national attention has to think seriously about marching to Beverly Hills with a begging bowl, and we are faced with the spectacle of United States Senators chasing money at gatherings of 22-year-old actors. At one such bash, Mr. Brownstein reports that a prominent young television actress, concerned about her tax bite, confronted Senator Alan Cranston and wanted to know if he could pass a law to give her some relief. The Senator's answer is unrecorded.    The grand, irreducible point about Hollywood is that it both creates and reflects the dreams and aspirations of the nation. Managing those dreams and aspirations, giving them life, is Washington's task. In bringing together the two endeavors, entertainment and politics, both so fundamentally American, in an astute and rewarding book, Mr. Brownstein has produced a match made in celluloid heaven.

title: The Shuberts Of Broadway
author: Brooks Mcnamara
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: Who were Sam, Jacob and Lee Shubert, and how did they come to play such a major role in creating the Broadway we know today? In THE SHUBERTS OF BROADWAY: A History Drawn From the Collections of the Shubert Archive (Oxford University, $35), Brooks McNamara, a professor of performance studies at New York University and director of the Shubert Archive, provides a detailed if somewhat bland history of the brothers and their phenomenal impact on the theater. Discarding their Yiddish, inventing middle initials, streamlining their personal histories (matters of age, birth order and place of origin were altered to suit), these sons of a peddler were brilliant entrepreneurs who saw opportunities for profit in the American passion for stage entertainment. Generously illustrated with photographs from the Shubert Archive, the book brims with lore about these colorful, ruthless and enigmatic brothers, as well as with details of the spectacular rise and subsequent ignominious decline of their immense theater empire. But Mr. McNamara's respectful, gee-whiz, only-in-America approach does not do justice to his subjects. Still, "The Shuberts of Broadway," an insider's authorized history, offers much in the way of information and memorabilia, and readers eager to know something of the three men whose name has become synonymous with Broadway today might find it right up their alley.

pull_quote: Musical performance, that most immediate and most ephemeral of the arts, isn't easily fixed into the solid stuff of reference books, and THE ART OF THE PIANO: Its Performers, Literature, and Recordings (Summit, $40) doesn't entirely overcome the strain between its form and its subject. title: Wayward Women: A Guide To Women Travellers

outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: The Victorian explorer Sir Samuel Baker was pleased to discover that his wife possessed "a share of sang-froid admirably adapted for African travel. Mrs. Baker is not a screamer." Neither are many of the roughly 350 other estimable ladies in Jane Robinson's WAYWARD WOMEN: A Guide to Women Travellers (Oxford University, $29.95). And neither, unfortunately, are they as well known as their male counterparts. Ms. Robinson, a British bibliographer, set out to correct this situation by producing a reference guide to "all the first-hand travel accounts ever written by women" and published in the English language. But then, luckily for the reader, she committed what she charmingly calls "the bibliographer's cardinal sin" -- she started to read the books themselves. The result is a less comprehensive but far more engaging work, an annotated ramble through a surprisingly large chunk of history in the company of ancient pilgrims (the fourth-century abbess Etheria, who, lacking a Baedeker, merely used her Bible to map a route through the Holy Land), modern daredevils (the Hon. Mrs. Victor Bruce, the first woman known to be charged with speeding, who was still test-driving for the Ford Motor Company at the age of 78) and eternal eccentrics (Margaret Fountaine, a parson's daughter whose "three great passions" were "travel, butterflies, and Unsuitable Attachments"). Ms. Robinson not only introduces us to such tempting (and often out of print) titles as "On Sledge and Horseback to Outcast Siberian Lepers," "Unprotected Females in Norway" and "To Lake Tanganyika in a Bath Chair"; she also steers us wittily away from bores like Charlotte Cameron ("the patron saint of cruise liners") and Mrs. Theodore F. Hughes (a late 19th-century visitor to the Orient who "grew maudlin and weak on a diet of chicken and oysters"). Any dedicated reader of travel books is bound to have a few quibbles with her selections (Lola Montez and Florence Nightingale, but no Sybille Bedford?), although sheer gratitude for discoveries like "An English Girl's First Impressions of Burmah" by Beth Ellis ("one of the funniest travel books ever written") is likely to win out.
